controls.title: Pasta Marketing, Magic Players, and Political Movements
controls.full_text:
tl;dr: I propose that we can classify movements into categories based on how their members relate to politics. Some approach politics as a way of achieving goals, and some approach politics as a way of relieving emotional impulses. The first kind of politics, however, is still downstream of some emotional impulse, just an extra step removed, because the impulse has been converted into a concrete goal by passing through a world-model.

Warning, this post contains some discussion of object-level politics, though I have tried to minimise it. I am also going to be trying to inhabit Richard Ngo's political frame a bit more than I normally would, so some parts of his frame with which I disagree, such as the choice of "Woke Left" vs "Tech Left" as the major split, I will leave be.

Richard Ngo says the following on Twitter

RichardMCNgo: Four analogies for a country:

1. The nationalist right views it as a family or community. So applying the same bar to citizens as to outsiders is nonsensical, because the country is of, by, and for its citizens.

2. The tech right views it as a company: you should bring in only the people who will benefit it. But this view is ultimately empty, because it doesn’t tell you what the interests of a country actually are. Hence the tech right (who are usually positive-sum thinkers) keep falling back on zero-sum concepts like “being competitive” or “winning against China” to justify their preferred policies. (Yarvin makes the “country as corporation” analogy particularly explicit.)

3. The tech left views it as a charity. To them, wanting others not to receive what you’re been given is hypocritical. This view is also empty, because it doesn’t tell you where the windfall actually comes from—and once you start to talk about the benefits of culture, ethics, institutions, etc, it becomes clear that citizens (and their ancestors) *built* that windfall rather than just being given it.

4. The woke left views it as a cancer: something that is aggressive and parasitic by its very nature. Countries are inherently violent (in asserting their borders) and exclusionary (of non-citizens) and therefore shouldn’t exist (or at least shouldn’t be allowed to police their borders, which is effectively the same thing). A charitable read is that this is a trauma reaction to the holocaust and colonialism—but regardless, it has become so deeply anti-civilization that it seems descriptively accurate to call it evil and insane.

...

I'm going to ignore most of this and just go off in my own direction. Leaving out the Nationalist Right for now, I think there's an interesting divide between the {Tech Left, Tech Right} cluster, and the {Woke Left} cluster here, and that Richard's model of the Woke Left is wrong because he's missing something.

...but before I can explain that I need to explain Magic The Gathering market research.

...but before that, I need to explain pasta sauce market research.

Tomato Sauce Marketing

This story is somewhat apocryphal, but here we go: back in the 1980s, Campbell's (the sauce guys) hired the psychophysicist (this is a real subdiscipline of psychology) Howard Moskowitz to improve their Prego tomato sauce brand. They just couldn't figure out the right formula, and their taste-testing results were all over the place. Sauces that seemed popular would lose on a taste-test to other sauces.

Moskowitz, allegedly, directed them make a bunch of different sauces, have a panel of testers rate all of them, and then looked at the data.

Turns out that to best serve the market, you want three different sauces: regular, spicy, and extra chunky. In particular, nobody was serving the market for extra chunky sauce. Campbell's filled the chunky sauce market niche, and did very well doing it.

Timmies, Johnnies, and Spikes

Magic The Gathering (the deck-building card game) did something similar. They also found three archetypical clusters of buyers, and, like Campbell's, resolved to serve all three clusters. For MtG, where you buy packs of cards without knowing their exact contents, this means that in each series of cards, there are a few cards geared towards each cluster of buyers.

The easiest one to explain is Spike. Spikes want to win. Spike wants cards which are useful for winning. This makes it quite easy to sell cards to Spike: if a card is good, then Spike wants it. One thing that Spike doesn't like is too much chaos. Spike wants predictability in their deck.

The next archetype is Johnny. Johnny wants to express creativity. A good card for Johnny is one which is kind of weird, but kind of good. Spike wants to win however possible. Johnny wants to win by combining three obscure and seemingly-useless cards in order to something something I don't play MtG.

Finally we get to Timmy. Timmy wants to have fun. Timmy wants to play the biggest, most bombastic card combinations. He enjoys winning, yes, but he'd rather have a few exciting wins than a bunch of boring ones.

I like the following anti-example of an unpopular card to illustrate the point:

Suppose you have a card with the following ability: when summoned, flip a coin. If heads, the card has eight attack, and one defense. If tails, the card has one attack and eight defense.

Spike doesn't like this, because it's random and he can't plan around it, so it's not very good. He'd prefer something like "when summoned, pick between one attack/eight defense, and eight attack/one defense."

Johnny doesn't like this, because the effect isn't interesting enough to express anything. He'd prefer something like "when summoned, swap the attack and defense of one card on your field".

Timmy doesn't like this, because the randomness is too balanced! He'd prefer a fifty-fifty chance of getting eight attack/eight defense, and one attack/one defense.

(I saw part of the above example in a talk somewhere and can't now find it)

To put it succinctly:

Timmy wants to feel something

Johnny wants to express something

Spike wants to win

Back to Politics

Here's a model which (I think) explains a lot of Richard's confusion.

The Tech Left and the Tech Right groups are both engaging with the political machinery of their country as a means towards achieving a goal. The Tech Left have a goal, something like "minimise suffering, maximise flourishing" and they see the American political machinery as one entity which can achieve that. Therefore, they disproportionately support things like foreign aid (which helps people where they are), immigration (which helps people by moving them to the US) as well as domestic policies that benefit existing citizens. Their political actions are then guided by what, under their model, helps them achieve these goals.

Likewise, the Tech Right has some kind of goal: a wealthy nation full of rich people, technological development, and cool stuff. In order for this to happen, they support getting skilled workers to immigrate (and, sometimes, less skilled workers, where this stimulates economic growth), and having less regulation.

I don't think a good model of the Woke Left is that they view nation states as a cancer and actively work to dismantle them. I think a better model is that you are making a kind of error when you consider them as trying to work towards a goal at all.

Some political movements are spikish. They appeal to people who are trying to achieve a goal and want to use politics to do that. Other political movements appeal to some kind of mix of Johnny and Timmy. I'll call them jimmish. jimmish movements appeal to people who want to use politics as an outlet for their emotions. What Richard sees as people on the Woke Left trying to, to paraphrase, destroy nation states as a concept, I see as people using politics as a direct outlet for the emotions they feel when they see people taking locally horrible actions.

Where Do We Get The Goals?

Of course, the goals of movements like the Tech Left and Tech Right don't come from nowhere. Most saliently, the Tech Left have built their altruistic goals from similar empathetic impulses as the ones from which the Woke Left have built theirs.

For any particular impulse, we can have a jimmish movement which directs that impulse towards politics-as-outlet. There might also be various spikish movements, which first use some kind of world-model to transmute that impulse into a goal, and then approach politics as a means towards that goal.

One rule of thumb is that spikish movements have a terrible track record of standing up to the jimmish movements which have grown from the same parent impulse. I suspect that this comes from a kind of internal sane-washing bias: we empathise with our jimmish counterparts, and project our reasonable (to ourselves) world-model-based action modes onto them.

The Second Transmutation

The above transmutation, of impulses into goals, makes sense. But there's a stranger transmutation that can happen. Sometimes, jimmish movements become highly strategic, towards an awful, awful version of a goal. Think "Environmentalists protest nuclear power" level bad. The environmentalists in question are really quite good at making sure we never get nuclear power, so they must have some kind of functioning world-model, but that world-model never lets them see that their own goal runs directly counter to their own impulses.

I don't quite know how this happens, but I can hazard a guess:

Your movement spews random impulsive outputs in all directions

Most of it does nothing

Occasionally, your impulses hit a weak spot in the world, and the world moves

This, on a lower level than the impulse itself, reinforces your movement towards spewing in that direction, because you satisfied the impulse.

Over time, the reinforcement towards satisfying the impulse turns your movement into a highly optimised machine for satisfying it's own impulse

Movements that do this well are better able to attract jimmish types

I guess this is like how, if you're lonely, you might transmute that into a plan to make friends, or you might transmute it into a set of behaviours which lead you to develop a parasocial relationship with a TikTok star and spend six hours a day online, which in fact hampers your ability to make friends.

Back To Ngo

I suspect that the most important split in organised political movements is whether they've performed the first transmutation, and turned their impulses into a plan to achieve an objective, thus appealing to spikish types, or performed the second transmutation, and become a machine for satisfying impulses directly, thus appealing to jimmish types.

There's a second set of questions as to i) whether you share the values implied by the impulses, and ii) whether you think the world-model of a spikish movement is good.

If I have to do some slightly unfair psychologising:

I think Ngo is a spikish type, and he has some reasonable impulses surrounding how a country should be organised. I think, like a lot of spikish types, he has a massive blind spot around the jimmish movement with those same impulses. I think this causes him to be biased towards Nationalist Right movements, despite those movements being, very often, highly jimmish and ineffective at their goals.

Coda: How Do You Tell If You're Jimmish?

I don't really know. There might be an internal feeling which corresponds to jimmish behaviour, and I can hazard something of a guess, but it's just a guess: I think that having a "hot" or "busy" mental state corresponds with jimmish impulses. That's it.

Coda 2: Are All Emotional Impulses Bad?

Probably not. I think, once you've verified that your feelings are rational, and you're really in a spikish way, you should try and really feel those impulses about the cause again. This is something that (IMO) EAs have done pretty well with on the global health front. I've met several people who really do seem to feel what $4000 per human life means.

controls.title: The right (and wrong) worries to have about water
controls.full_text:
[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!M3AT!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2eca632e-14eb-4e11-95d4-2126a27b41a2_1456x292.webp]]

In grade school we were  taught that water is a renewable resource that covers most of the planet and, quite literally, falls from the sky. I remember water cycle posters from second grade: a storm cloud that dropped rain in the mountains, which collected into rivers, which flowed into lakes or oceans, whereupon the water evaporated to form a new storm cloud. The point was that water moves through this cycle but is never used up. Despite that immutable bit of Earth science, modern society has long been preoccupied with the fear that our water resources are on borrowed time, as though we might accidentally turn the entire planet into a desert.

This fear is pervasive in mass media. The movie Chinatown was released in 1974 and the villain who secures a monopoly over life-giving water has since become an archetype. In Rango from 2011, the rich water thief is an evil folksy tortoise. James Bond gets in on the trope in Quantum of Solace. The 2015 film The Big Short is ostensibly about the 2008 financial crisis but ends with an ominous description of investors shifting their focus to water.

If these examples speak to a moderate anxiety, more apocalyptic options are available. There are now five Mad Max movies set in Australia, with water becoming more precious in each iteration. In Tank Girl from 1995, you can watch Malcolm McDowell rule a desert world — Australia again — and kill his enemies by desiccating them with a spiky suction cup (apropos of nothing, that movie is partially animated because they somehow forgot to film about 10 scenes). In the New York Times bestseller The Water Knife, water rights — which can apparently be carried around like bearer bonds — are worth killing over and somehow still enforceable in a dystopia.

In public policy discussions, our fears can manifest in odd ways. We worry about almond farming (a thirsty high-value crop) but not alfalfa (a very thirsty low-value crop). We worry about evaporative water loss from data centers in Virginia (a region with a near inexhaustible supply of fresh water) but we also put water-guzzling golf courses in Phoenix (a desert).

How did we come to be so incoherent? We worry about a crisis that doesn’t exist while doing very little to reform water management institutions. Less panic and more moderate bureaucratic change (riveting solution, I know) could make us richer while improving the environment.

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!zbwd!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F88f50032-73c2-4c5f-a73e-197277f03cf5_800x640.jpeg]]

Source

Importing each other’s water problems

For most of human history, freshwater concerns revolved around agriculture. Things were fine as long as there was enough water to grow crops. Some cultures, like the Khmer Empire, came up with ingenious solutions for water management but were still undone by changing weather patterns. Often, however, civilizations arose in areas where the supply of water relative to possible uses was effectively unlimited.

This was the case when the eastern U.S. was first settled by Europeans. One didn’t need to worry about water at all since the amount available was so vast relative to any possible use for it. In fact, as the historian Anthony Carlson describes in Perilous Waters, we spent many decades preoccupied with draining freshwater wetlands to create more farms. The term “reclamation” initially referred to reclaiming swampland, rather than reclaiming water for arid regions.

The military explorers Stephen Long and Zebulon Pike popularized a notion that the Great Plains were a “great American desert,” incapable of supporting agriculture.

The situation changed with the turn of the last century, when we became capable of fouling water at scale. Our first foolproof plan to deal with water pollution was to ignore it. As described by the historian Mike Wallace in Greater Gotham, New York City’s industries operated on the assumption that tides simply carried away any pollutants. The city tested this with dye at one point, realized it wasn’t true at all, then… kept dumping sludge in the rivers. Today, some of the city’s waterways are EPA Superfund sites and the billions of oysters that once lined its bay are long dead. Despite localized disasters, society maintained the belief that we couldn’t possibly damage water resources at a large scale. One could simply go to Long Island to see clean water.

It was in the drier West that we had to worry about getting enough water for the first time. The military explorers Stephen Long and Zebulon Pike popularized a notion that the Great Plains were a “great American desert,” incapable of supporting agriculture. Pike especially was relieved due to his concerns that American democracy might not be sustainable across too vast a geographic expanse, noted historian of the American West Patricia Limerick in an interview.

Humans turned out to be ingenious engineers and simply built our way around nature’s constraints. Water is seasonal in the West, so in the 1800s we began assembly of a vast infrastructure to store and distribute it, eventually enabling large-scale agriculture. We were so enthralled with our success that we seemed to forget any constraints existed.

In the early 20th century, western water reclamation projects — this time, with “reclamation” coming to mean capturing and retaining water, rather than draining it to make swampland arable — kicked into high gear. Eastern congressmen were initially “not willing to tax the farmers” of their own states to take western lands “and convert them into sugar-producing lands.” But opposition was short-lived and congress created the Bureau of Reclamation in 1902. By the 1930s, the government was addressing agricultural surpluses on one hand (by paying farmers to take land out of production) while, with the other, building reclamation projects that would put more land into cultivation.

Meanwhile, the East and West seemed eager to import each other’s problems. It was puzzling enough that Eastern cities consistently placed sewage lines next to their freshwater intake sites, according to Limerick — but it was even more strange that, learning nothing from the failures back east, Western cities did the same, ending up with their own pollution issues.

Nonetheless, there was an unshakable belief in engineering our way out of anything.

Mistakes, mistakes, mistakes

So it happened that optimism veered into recklessness. Nationwide, we polluted with abandon, exemplified by the time Cleveland set the Cuyahoga River on fire in 1969 — the “mistake on the lake” — and managed to get a Lake Erie reference in the Lorax by doing so. (Point of fact, we set that river on fire at least 13 times, but the 1969 one received national attention.)

Out West, it was as though any sort of water conservation counted as defeatism. The tragedy is that this era’s engineering feats were remarkable! We built an industrial economy and did manage to enable farming in a region that should’ve been too dry for it. But then we deluded ourselves into thinking we’d never have to care about where our water comes from.

In Science Be Dammed, Eric Kuhn and John Fleck describe how, starting with the Colorado River Compact in 1922, we’ve consistently allocated more water than the river has. Crucially, this was never an honest mistake: Before the compact was signed, U.S. Geological Survey hydrologist E.C. LaRue famously warned that water level projections were being rosily based on an unusually wet period. He was ignored.

Even more gob-smacking examples of self-deception are available. The Dust Bowl by Ken Burns explains how farmers fatuously assumed bumper rains would last forever during the anomalously wet 1920s. They undertook a “Great Plow-up,” tilling vast tracts of prairie grasses — which had adapted to uncertain rainfall over eons — and replacing them with drought-intolerant crops. The resulting ecological catastrophe was the second time the region’s homesteaders got burned: In the 1800s, they’d told themselves that “rain follows the plow” (i.e., planting a region will make it rain there) until an 1890s drought proved them wrong.

The problem of water quality first captured national attention insofar as it affected drinking water. In The Search for the Ultimate Sink, historian Joel Tarr explains that water quality was seen as a public health problem and “solved” by treating only our incoming drinking water. Of course, treating drinking water made us much healthier (I, for one, am happy to have never had cholera), but it did nothing to keep industrial waste from our waterways.

Out West, it was as though any sort of water conservation counted as defeatism.

If anything, it made that problem worse because it meant less political pressure on polluters. Things shifted by the middle of the 20th century, as society came to view water pollution more in environmental than epidemiological terms, thanks to new and more visible chemical pollutants, like synthetic organic chemicals that could add thick layers of foam to rivers.

We became gradually more conscious of the problem of water scarcity as we ran out of low-hanging fruit for irrigation projects. Sensibly enough, the best western reclamation sites — dams, reservoirs, irrigation canals — were built out first, so each additional one was more and more marginal. By the 1970s, additional projects just didn’t make any financial sense; by the 1980s (the canonical book on the topic, Cadillac Desert, was published in 1986) we started to see the downsides of our century-long water management spree. These drawbacks included mineral accumulation on irrigated land, pushing animal species to the brink (it’s very difficult for salmon to spawn in a dammed river), and overdrawing the Colorado so persistently that it would no longer reach the sea.

Also, we just got richer. This explanation for why we started to care about water management (and any environmental issues really) can be attributed to more than a few academics, notably among them historian Samuel Hays and economists Gene Grossman and Alan Krueger. Perhaps that’s because it’s obvious in retrospect: A wealthier society has more attention and resources to devote to the environment. It’s easier to care about whether salmon can spawn when one isn’t worried about contracting typhoid from the municipal water supply.

We began to fix our mistakes. On pollution, the Clean Water Act in 1972 marked the point where we got serious about the problem. The act federalized standards, imposed limits on “point sources” of pollution (e.g., a “point source” might be the pipe dumping sludge from a particular factory), and it provided vast sums of money to fund municipal sewage treatment.

On scarcity, there was no, shall I say, watershed moment. Rather, there were various marginal changes that made an impact over time. Urban areas made real progress on demand management, so much so that total usage fell despite large population gains in the southwest1. Federal plumbing standards helped in this regard. (Anyone who has come across the odd dive bar with a pre-standards-era toilet can attest that they use something like an Olympic swimming pool worth of water to flush). Additionally, some water was reallocated from agricultural to urban uses, and farmers began to use water more efficiently (though there is still much work to be done on both of those fronts).

As a result, water quality today is much better than in the 1970s. Water scarcity is still an open issue, but the West has managed to avoid essentially all of the dire predictions from the 1980s: Instead of running dry, cities greatly reduced per capita water use; aquifer depletion didn’t make farming impossible so much as force us to substitute crops; the speed of sedimentation (which fills in reservoirs making them ineffective over long timescales) was vastly overstated; and salinization of farmland proved to be something of a manageable headwind rather than a catastrophe.

The trouble is that our perceptions are stuck in the era of burning rivers. Pollution is still a concern everywhere, but these days mostly from agricultural runoff, which looms large now simply because we’ve been so successful at addressing industrial waste. Outside of periodic droughts, water scarcity is mostly a concern in arid regions. Even in arid regions, and even with climate change, there is a vast amount of water available. Conservation is good for the environment and, in the long run, would make farming more sustainable, but cities just are not going to run out of water for human consumption.

What’s left to worry about today?

So, what exactly are the water management problems we face today? I sat down with several resource economists and a water policy specialist to find out.

Brian Gray, an expert on water law at the Public Policy Institute of California, told me that the federal Clean Water Act and state-level water quality laws have significantly reduced municipal and industrial water pollution, at least from his vantage point as a California specialist. Nationally, we’ve seen a marked improvement as quantified by researchers David Keiser and Joseph Shapiro.

That said, an improvement does not imply full success. As a New Yorker, I’ll note that the Gowanus Canal remediation has been in progress for nearly two decades and the plan for mitigating the city’s combined sewer is scheduled for geologic timescales. My sarcasm aside, Gray stressed that the federal law explicitly exempts agricultural sources of pollution (i.e., runoff) from regulation because these were thought impractical to measure (being diffuse rather than “point” sources of contaminants).

Agricultural pollution mostly entails phosphorus and nitrogen; these aren’t industrial toxins but the ecological impact is quite large. The EPA rates over 40% of streams in poor condition for these nutrients, which harms wildlife (the chemicals cause algae blooms, which can, among other things, leave water hypoxic). The effect on human health is more difficult to quantify: It’s unclear exactly how bad high phosphate exposure is and it can be tricky to measure how many people are exposed. That noted, exposure rates seem to be small and concentrated among households with private wells.

These constitute a gap in our remediation efforts but there’s cause for hope on that front: Gray said that many farms, especially in California, use canals and pipes for drainage, which makes tracking pollution more feasible. California, for one, is beginning to regulate these discharges under state law.

The resource economists I spoke with — Eric Edwards at UC Davis, Nick Hagerty at Montana State University, and Jonathan Yoder at Washington State University — all focused on Western water rights, simply because water scarcity, while occasionally an issue in the East, is ubiquitous and more severe in the West.

A common refrain from them was that it is often enormously difficult to actually trade water rights, meaning that even though the arid West still has a lot of water, an overly complex system makes us  inefficient at allocating it. Simplifying the process would make it easier for cities to grow, allow farmers to profit from the sale of their water rights, and would allow us to leave more water for the environment.

Briefly, a water right is the right to do something with a water source. The right may specify use (e.g., consumption of water, diversion of a stream, etc.), point of use (that is, exactly where the water may be drawn), quantity of water, return requirements (how much water must be returned to the source after use), and so on.

In the U.S., water rights fall into two main categories: The first is riparian, under which water rights are tied to land abutting a water source; with this regime people are allowed “reasonable use” and rights are usufructuary, meaning land owners have a right to the water but do not legally own it. This type of right is the default in the East.

The second category, prior appropriation, is common in the West. Under that doctrine, rights are not tied to the land. For instance, one may own a plot of land but not have the right to place a well on said land — to do so, you’d need to purchase the relevant water rights. Prior appropriation rights are based on seniority, which means, if I ignore a lot of nuance, one owns a senior right if he or she happens to have an ancestor who first came along and put a water source to a “beneficial use”. Riparian rights tend to work best where there’s a lot of water to go around, which explains why the West uses a different doctrine.

Riparian rights are straightforward: One acquires the right with a parcel of land. So the market for them is just the land marker. Thus, when we talk about water markets, we’re usually referring to prior appropriation rights. In a prior appropriation water rights market, one may theoretically purchase rights to water, but the process is rarely straightforward.

Edwards explained that if a large city wanted to increase its water supply, the matter isn’t so simple as just using the municipal budget to purchase water. For one, many farmers have water rights but cannot sell them because rights are often collectively managed by water districts that coordinate among farmers. If the city finds willing sellers, the two parties cannot simply agree to the transfer. Other farmers could protest that changing water diversion patterns would impact them. Such issues often end up in court. The process is so Byzantine that water brokers exist to work through the bureaucracy, and, of course, they have to be paid.

The end result is a huge gap between what a buyer pays for rights and what a seller might receive. Yoder said the economic literature is “full of transaction cost estimates” estimated to be roughly 1/3 the value of a sale.

In some places, it’s not just transaction costs and market frictions gumming up the works. The Colorado River Basin is perhaps the biggest water management problem we have right now. Yoder noted the initial over-allocation means that we’ve just fought over the water rights since. It’s difficult to even talk about transferring water rights if there’s uncertainty over which states’ initial claims will win out. How can something be transferred if we can’t even agree who controls it?

None of the economists advocated a completely deregulated system. After all, a large share of western water disbursements are managed by the federal government. Plus, when we talk about trading water rights, we’re often considering public entities acquiring them from one another. Does a public utility in Phoenix need a given amount of water or should it go to a public utility in San Diego? The point is that a functioning market for water could allow the cities to trade effectively (with each other and with farmers), ensuring neither suffers in a drought.

What of more science-fiction sounding solutions? Perhaps we’ll succeed in making electricity so cheap that large scale desalination is practical? Well, no. Hagerty allowed that it’s a “potentially exciting option, particularly valuable for reducing urban water uncertainty, but depends a whole lot on how cheap electricity could get.”

But, water is heavy and slippery and, thus, expensive to transport. Even if desalination were free, piping it from the coast for agriculture would be hugely expensive relative to moderate changes in our water management institutions. Hagerty added that, right now, having to use desalination in California represents a “huge policy failure” because it’s just so expensive relative to the water we already have. It seems working amicably together is still our best option for managing the most salient of natural resources.

Overall then, our water management problems can be attributed to misaligned incentives and rickety market mechanisms. Boring bureaucratic details.  So why, instead of reasonable technocratic changes, were people being hectored to stop drinking almond milk a few years ago? Why are the papers filled with articles about data center water use now? Why so much paranoia? And, above all, why do people seem to worry about a lack of water instead of a misallocation of the vast amounts of water we already have?

Yoder suggested a status quo bias, explaining that soda-pop bottling plants have faced local resistance too. People worry about new water withdrawals. The specter of a single “data center” industry also gives a nationalized face to what were once just various local fights over commercial water use. At my prodding, Yoder agreed that the public “often lacks a sense of scale.” Hagerty said, “one of the biggest problems is that a lot of journalists are not quantitatively literate.”

In an effort to prove myself the exception, here’s some arithmetic: The thirstiest data center in the world uses about 1 billion gallons of water per year by evaporating it for cooling. (It uses the same type of HVAC system as large apartment or office buildings) That’s enough to grow about one square mile of alfalfa, which is used for cattle feed. That amount of feed would translate to getting about 500 head of cattle to slaughter weight, not counting feed for the breeding herd. There were over 27 million head of beef cows in the U.S. at the start of this year and the U.S. grows over 22,000 square miles of alfalfa each year.

Now consider our most-stressed large water system. The Colorado River Basin flows at, on average since 2000, 12.4 million acre-feet of water each year, or over 4 trillion gallons. The difference between a billion and a trillion is difficult for humans to comprehend, but a billion seconds makes just over 31 years, a trillion makes over 31,000. We consume 13.1 million acre-feet from the Colorado.

The gap we need to close is actually less than 0.7 million acre-feet because of inflows along the river. This isn’t an insurmountable problem; it’s 114,000 cows; we have 27 million of them, not counting milk cows, the breeding herd, and calves.

I asked Edwards, Hagerty, and Yoder about their outlooks for our future. Since we’ve already reclaimed just about all the water we feasibly can, Edwards explained that the available water is a zero-sum proposition but the value we get from it certainly isn’t. “I think there are 1,000 different things people would do to become more efficient, from switching crops or deficit irrigation at low cost all the way up to high cost xeriscaping and rain barrel installation,” he said.

Yoder mentioned policy options that can work well in some circumstances, such as water banks, which allow rights holders to forgo a water withdrawal and “bank” the right to do so in the future. He also sees promise in emerging technologies to reduce regulatory and transaction costs, which would make re-allocating water less cumbersome.

Hagerty focused on the status quo at first, explaining that, even in developing countries with institutions far worse than our own, authorities tend to act in time to ensure adequate water supplies. The counterexamples are well-publicized simply because they are so anomalous. He followed up to explain that we have the option of continuing as we have, but that doing might squander so much potential:

“I think we will continue to muddle through most water scarcity challenges despite our brittle institutions for water management, but I think a lot of these discussions are missing another big issue — it’s not just about how much urban areas will have to cut their water use, it’s also about what our urban areas could look like if more water were available for them. If we had more water, how much housing could be built in some of the most productive, most desirable, and lowest-emission cities in the country? How many people are missing the chance to have a better job, more opportunities, a better life? How many new cities would be built in the Southwest if there were more water for people? We don’t know exactly, but it might be a really big deal — it’s plausible it outweighs all the other problems we tend to think about with water management.”

For my part, I think our unrelenting negativity on this issue is almost the mirror image of our grandparents’ confidence. In both cases, many people have  refused to engage with reality or admit that trade-offs must be made. One writer I interviewed for this piece was incredulous when I suggested we may need to set priorities between competing concerns, abruptly ending the meeting and asking not to be quoted here.

However, insisting that we focus on everything at once has a lot in common with refusing to worry about anything: Either way, we excuse ourselves from necessary action. The fact of the matter remains that theatrics — like banning data centers in water-rich New York — will not add one drop of water to the Colorado River. What’s more, there’s no arch villain trying to hold our cities’ drinking water hostage. The truth is more banal: Voters, and farmers, and policy makers are being a bit emotional and a bit short-sighted. We could make things easier for ourselves and the environment if we’d address water management like adults.

Lawrence Costa is an economist who writes about trains and operas on Substack because he lacks interpersonal skills. His research has focused on housing, labor markets, and education. He once went to Scranton (inadvertently).

1There is a huge disparity between the value farmers place on water (low) and what cities do (relatively high). Cities could really use some additional water, but it’s a pretty reasonable amount; agriculture will remain the largest user by a wide margin.

controls.title: How Accurate Have AI Progress Forecasts Been So Far?
controls.full_text:
This is the first post in a short series on the accuracy of AI progress forecasts we’ve gathered at the Forecasting Research Institute (FRI). In the next post, we’ll explore how to improve the accuracy and relevance of AI forecasts in our studies going forward.

This post was authored by Josh Rosenberg, Matt Reynolds, Nadja Flechner, and Zack Devlin-Foltz.1

Summary

Since mid-2022, FRI has collected forecasts on AI progress across many projects. In this post, we cover results so far on how accurate experts and superforecasters have been at forecasting AI progress across a range of indicators: benchmarks and non-benchmark capability tests, adoption and diffusion metrics, social impacts, and geopolitics and governance.

In brief, across our studies, forecasters dramatically underestimate AI progress on benchmarks, have a more mixed track record on AI adoption and diffusion though often lean toward underestimation, and there is not yet enough evidence to assess their track record on predicting macro-scale economic and societal impacts of AI.

There are some examples of forecasters overestimating AI-related progress. In a mid-2025 study they overestimated the impact of LLMs on improving amateurs’ ability to do dangerous biology tasks, and the median expert looks very likely to have majorly overestimated how widespread the use of autonomous vehicles would be by the end of 2027.

Forecasts on some benchmarks (e.g., Chinese model performance on the Epoch Capabilities Index) and some diffusion-related questions (e.g., the rate of data center growth) appear on track to be broadly accurate.

There are some important limitations to keep in mind with these findings. For example:

We discuss many questions that have resolved early because AI milestones were reached sooner than expected, but highlighting these early-resolving questions may introduce bias, since by definition we do not have data on late-resolving questions. This may lead us toward identifying more areas where forecasters have underestimated AI progress rather than those where they have been accurate or overestimated progress.

For some unresolved questions we have used LLM projections to draw tentative accuracy conclusions—by their nature, these projections are more speculative.2 We plan to continue to publish accuracy updates over time, particularly for our Longitudinal Expert AI Panel (LEAP).

In the next post in this series, we’ll discuss how we might improve the accuracy and relevance of LEAP forecasts.

Introduction

There is major disagreement and uncertainty about the trajectory of AI progress, with thoughtful and engaged researchers looking at similar evidence and drawing very different conclusions. For example, Ajeya Cotra and Timothy B. Lee disagree by about 40 years on when they expect self-sufficient AI systems to exist. Andrej Karpathy has argued that achieving AGI would have little to no impact on GDP, while Epoch researchers have modeled that AI automation could lead to economic growth in excess of 30% a year.3 These disagreements are large, but even they only capture a relatively narrow section of the huge range of views that exist on AI progress.

At the Forecasting Research Institute, we want to bring more rigor to the AI progress discussion and help policymakers understand where we’re headed. We have been eliciting forecasts on AI progress since our Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament in mid-2022 and have continued to gather AI progress forecasts in specific domains, including biorisk and cyber. In mid-2025 we launched the Longitudinal Expert AI Panel (LEAP)—a monthly survey that gathers AI progress forecasts from a panel of leading experts and superforecasters. We want to clarify what’s likely to happen with the future of AI, help people understand where forecasts are more or less reliable, and identify particularly accurate forecasting approaches that might give us more insight on the future.

In this post, we’ll provide an update on how accurate forecasters—both domain experts and generalist forecasters with a strong track record (”superforecasters”)—have been across FRI studies. In the next post in this series, we’ll take a look at a few different approaches to improving the accuracy and relevance of LEAP forecasts.

Methodology

In this post, we considered forecasts across all relevant FRI studies from mid-2022 to August 2026: our Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament (XPT) and initial XPT follow-up, AI adversarial collaboration, LLM-biorisk study and Active Site RCT forecasting study, AI-cyber risk pilot, Forecasting the Economic Effects of AI, and the Longitudinal Expert AI Panel (LEAP).4

In our summary of findings below, we highlight a subset of forecasts that we believe are broadly illustrative of the core trends we have observed across studies. The number of actual AI forecasting questions across all of our studies is much larger than what we cover in this post. We focused on a reasonably representative subset of questions to keep this post simpler and more concise, which meant making subjective choices about which forecasts to include or exclude. In general, we included questions where there were either known resolution values or other data that gave us some indication of whether forecasters were on track to be accurate or not.

You can view all of the forecasts that informed this analysis in this table: Forecaster Accuracy on Selected AI Progress Questions and compare those to the full set of AI progress questions we’ve elicited across projects.

We split our AI progress forecasts into four main categories: capabilities, adoption, impacts, and geopolitics and governance:

Capabilities: Predictions about AI performance on benchmarks or other clearly defined tasks. For example: performance on FrontierMath; when AI will solve a Millennium Prize Problem; when a robot will successfully complete the “Coffee Test.”

Adoption: Predictions about the diffusion and adoption of AI in “real-world” settings. For example: the fraction of work hours assisted by AI; the proportion of adults reporting AI companion use; the global supply of industrial robots.

Impact: Predictions about the impact of AI on key outcomes. For example: entry-level tech hiring; GDP growth and labor force participation rate; life expectancy; AI’s place on the Technological Richter Scale.

Geopolitics and governance of AI, including on autonomous cyber operations, frontier AI chip manufacturing, and governance of AI models.

AI progress is moving quickly, so we believe it is useful to provide an interim update on accuracy, but many questions in our studies have not yet resolved. To allow us to assess the quality of forecasts beyond those that have already resolved, this preliminary accuracy assessment also compares forecasts to:

Observed current values (prior to question resolution dates): for some questions, particularly benchmarks, we compare forecasts to the latest data that meets our resolution criteria, even if a question has not yet resolved.

LLM projections: We used GPT-5.5 with “high” reasoning to project the resolution of questions using last known data points, current reporting, and reasonable extrapolations.5 We ran these LLM projections in August 2026.

In this analysis, we mostly compare median forecasts from experts and superforecasters to resolution data, observed values, and LLM projections. (Note that the group of “experts” providing forecasts varies between studies.6) This approach allows us to identify where median forecasts majorly diverge from observed data and possible resolutions, but it does have some major limitations:

Focusing on median forecasts may obscure more accurate predictions from subsets of forecasters.

Our methodology is biased toward identifying underestimates of AI progress rather than overestimates. As soon as a real-world value crosses the median forecast threshold, that forecast is revealed to be too low. In contrast, a forecast can only be confirmed as too high once its resolution date has passed. Therefore, interim checks on accuracy (of the kind we do in this post) highlight underestimates while overestimates are harder to identify.

For most questions, we are not able to draw firm conclusions on accuracy in either direction.

Finally, a note on the “domain experts” discussed below. Our goal in our research was to recruit the kinds of experts that policymakers would typically turn to for advice on these topics. So, we typically include highly cited and well-credentialed domain experts.

Some illustrative examples are:

Our initial LEAP sample included 339 experts: 76 computer scientists, 76 AI industry experts, 68 economists, and 119 AI policy researchers. Twelve experts were AI TIME 100 honorees. Of the 76 computer scientists, 30 were professors at top-20 institutions (according to CSRankings.org) and 10 were among the 200 top-cited authors in AI (according to OpenAlex). Of the 76 AI industry employees, 26% worked for one of five leading AI companies (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, and Nvidia), and the median respondent had 9,100 citations (for the 59% of panelists for whom data is available).

In our study on the economic effects of AI, we recruited 69 economists. Of these, 58% had at least 1,000 citations and 37% had at least one “Top Five” journal publication.

In our study on LLM-enabled biorisk, we surveyed 46 subject-matter experts in biology and biosecurity. Of the experts, 27 (59%) reported expertise in both biosecurity and wet lab biology research. The expert group’s median number of years of experience was seven years for biosecurity work and eight years for wet lab research. Most experts had a doctorate (78%).

Capabilities

Across all of our AI progress work, forecasts on benchmark performance give us the clearest picture of forecaster accuracy so far. This is largely because more benchmark forecasts have resolved than any other type of forecast.

A clear trend is apparent from these resolved forecasts: the median expert and superforecaster tend to dramatically underestimate AI progress on benchmarks. This pattern is clear in earlier forecasts (from 2022) and those elicited as recently as spring 2026.

Below, we walk through several core examples that illustrate this pattern.

Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament (XPT)

In our mid-2022 Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament (XPT) we collected forecasts about AI progress on the MATH, MMLU, QuALITY, and IMO Gold Medal benchmarks. The chart below shows the implied probability the median domain expert and superforecaster assigned to the observed benchmark results. Overall, superforecasters assigned an average probability of just 9.7% to the observed outcomes across these four AI benchmarks, compared to 24.6% from domain experts. Forecasters were particularly surprised by AI achieving International Mathematical Olympiad gold-level performance in July 2025—this happened five years earlier than the median expert prediction (2030) and 10 years earlier than the median superforecaster prediction (2035).7

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!p23K!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fdfef61af-02bd-4eaf-9e35-a7202e3e1612_2048x1024.png]]

Figure 1: Superforecasters’ and domain experts’ predicted probabilities of observed progress on AI benchmarks. Probabilities were calculated based on the estimated probability density functions and the observed resolution values.

There is an obvious hypothesis for why XPT forecasters underestimated benchmark progress: they gave their forecasts between June and October 2022, before the public release of ChatGPT. But if we look to more recent forecasts, this pattern of underestimating benchmark progress continues.8

AI-bio and AI-cyber benchmarks

In our study on LLM-enabled biorisk, which collected forecasts between November 2024 and February 2025, superforecasters and subject-matter experts in biology and biosecurity substantially underestimated AI progress on biorisk-related benchmarks. For example, the median expert predicted that AI models would match a top virologist team on a troubleshooting benchmark (”VCT”) in 2030 while the median superforecaster thought it would take until 2034.9 In fact, AI models likely matched this baseline as of April 2025, several months after the survey was conducted. We also saw similar underestimation of AI progress on a cybersecurity benchmark (Cybench) in our study on LLM-enabled cybersecurity risk.

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!W9eT!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5d916d60-494f-4cf2-bf2a-f1ab3a6e3b64_1772x922.png]]

Table 1: Forecasts on biosecurity and cyber benchmarks from “Forecasting LLM-enabled Biorisk“ and “Forecasting AI Cyber Risks and Capabilities.”

Several related benchmark questions from these studies remain unresolved, such as, AI reaching a 90% success rate at helping non-experts to acquire synthetic DNA, AI enabling plausible bioweapon attack plans, and AI enabling novice hackers to match an elite team.10 To see all relevant forecasts from these studies, see the appendix table of all relevant AI progress questions.

Longitudinal Expert AI Panel (LEAP)

Since mid-2025 we’ve collected AI progress forecasts from a broad sample of experts (computer scientists, economists, AI industry experts, and AI policy experts) and superforecasters as part of the Longitudinal Expert AI Panel (LEAP). Both groups have substantially underestimated progress on math and coding benchmarks.

We asked forecasters to predict the highest performance on the benchmarks FrontierMath and LiveCodeBench Pro (Hard).11 The FrontierMath question resolved at the end of 2025, with the median forecaster in both groups underestimating progress. The LiveCodeBench Pro question resolves at the end of 2026, but the current state-of-the-art is so far ahead of forecaster medians that it is already clear that they have massively underestimated AI performance on this benchmark.12

The median expert predicted that the leading AI model on FrontierMath Tiers 1–3 by the end of 2025 would achieve 31%, while the median superforecaster predicted 30%. In reality, this question resolved at 40.7%.13 On LiveCodeBench Pro (Hard), the median expert forecast state-of-the-art performance of 14% by the end of 2026, while superforecasters predicted 12%. In May 2026 the actual state-of-the-art on this benchmark was 53.8%.

Forecasters also significantly underestimated performance on a question we asked in the fall of 2025 about the performance of closed-weight models across three benchmarks (FrontierMath Tiers 1–3 and 4, SWE-Bench Verified, and ARC-AGI-2). Forecasts for the open-weight portion of this question were much more accurate than those for the closed-weight portion, with the median of both groups predicting 20% mean benchmark performance against a resolution of 22.7%.14

In April–May 2026, we asked LEAP panelists to forecast the longest METR 80% time horizon listed for an AI model by the end of 2026. Experts and superforecasters gave forecasts of 3.4 and 3.5 hours, respectively. On May 8, toward the end of the survey period, METR updated the benchmark to show that Anthropic’s Mythos Preview model had achieved an estimated 80% time horizon of 3 hours and 6 minutes (3.1 hours), already within the range of median panelists’ forecasts for the end of 2026. If the historical trend of progress on this benchmark continues, forecasters’ median predictions will have substantially underestimated progress by the end of 2026.

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!PXCV!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F37c5bd91-8915-4af5-aefd-ae8a231e90e3_1980x1171.png]]

Figure 2: Expert and superforecaster predictions of state-of-the-art on the METR 80% time horizon benchmark by the end of 2026. The dotted line shows an extrapolation of the METR trend line to the resolution date. The bars on the expert and superforecaster predictions indicate the range of the 25th to 75th percentile of median outcome forecasts in each group.

While we were drafting this post, the news broke that OpenAI had likely solved one of the Millennium Prize Problems—the Navier-Stokes Problem–using an internal model significantly more capable than GPT-6 Astra. LEAP experts, originally forecasting in August to September 2025, gave just a 10% chance of AI solving a Millennium Prize Problem by the end of 2027, while superforecasters gave even lower odds of 5.4%. Although it is not completely clear whether the current situation meets our resolution criteria, it appears likely that these forecasts are another significant example of forecasters underestimating AI progress.

Exceptions: more accurate forecasts

Accuracy on some unresolved benchmark questions looks more promising. For example, according to our LLM projections, near-term forecasts on Chinese model performance on the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI) may be fairly accurate, although later resolution dates diverge more strongly from LLM forecasts.15

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!qIPj!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2f321880-53e1-4f0d-8937-107ed33c4836_1680x1046.png]]

Figure 3: Median expert and superforecaster predictions for the top-performing Chinese AI model on the Epoch Capabilities Index at various resolution dates. The gray bar represents an LLM projection of the same forecast. The error bars show the median p25 to median p75 forecast for experts and superforecasters.

Overestimation of a non-benchmark capability: AI-biorisk uplift study

We have fewer examples of non-benchmark capability forecasts, but one notable overestimation of AI capabilities came when forecasters predicted how much mid-2025 LLMs could help non-experts with biorisk-relevant laboratory tasks.

In mid-2025, we asked for predictions about what fraction of STEM undergraduates would be able to complete three biorisk-relevant tasks with the help of an LLM in a randomized controlled trial run by Active Site. Biosecurity experts (at median) predicted that 22.5% of the sample would complete the tasks, virologists predicted 40%, and superforecasters predicted 16.2%. In actuality, 5.2% of the sample completed all of the tasks.

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8xWV!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F79511382-c9ae-4357-aa66-19008b225427_7200x6000.png]]

Figure 4: Forecasts vs. actual RCT results, split by forecaster type. The box plots show the median and interquartile range of forecasts for each group of forecasters. The red dotted line shows the actual RCT result, with the red shaded area showing the 95% confidence interval of those results.

We discuss the potential implications of these findings about AI capabilities forecasting accuracy in the discussion section below.

AI adoption and diffusion

Adoption and diffusion forecasts attempt to track the uptake of AI through a range of proxies, including economic indicators, infrastructure rollout, and usage indicators. We have fewer resolved questions in this category and less observed data, so we are more reliant here on comparisons to LLM projections. As such, preliminary conclusions in this section are more speculative than our findings on benchmarks.

The forecasts below primarily come from LEAP, where we have collected the most adoption-related forecasts. In some highlighted cases we also have relevant data from the XPT.

Overall, the picture for forecasting accuracy on AI adoption and diffusion indicators is more mixed, though forecasters often lean toward underestimation:

On economic proxies for adoption, such as revenue growth of AI companies, median experts and superforecasters majorly underestimated progress.

On broad adoption indicators, such as what percentage of work hours in the US are assisted by AI, the evidence of forecaster accuracy is uncertain.

Forecasts for resources relevant to AI growth that are proxies for adoption and diffusion (electricity used by AI and data center growth) were much closer to LLM projections than other adoption indicators. However, in our XPT study, forecasters substantially underestimated how quickly spending on the largest models would grow.

It appears that experts overestimated the rate of autonomous vehicle adoption: when surveyed in June–August 2025, the median expert predicted that 7.3% of US ride-hailing trips would be completed by autonomous vehicles by the end of 2027. Based on current trends, LLMs predict that the actual resolution value will be 2.5%. Superforecasters appear more accurate, with a median forecast of 2%.

We have collected forecasts for many adoption and diffusion indicators that we cannot yet judge the accuracy of, such as what fraction of people will use AI for companionship over time and what share of drug sales will come from AI-discovered drugs.

Economic proxies for adoption: major underestimation of AI revenue growth

Broadly, forecasts of economic proxies for adoption seem to have significantly underestimated AI uptake.

In our study “Forecasting the Economic Effects of AI,” we asked participants for the highest annual recurring revenue (ARR) for an AI-focused company at the end of 2026. AI experts gave a median ARR of $20 billion, economists predicted $16 billion, and superforecasters predicted $25 billion.16 It is likely that the current value for this question (as of September 22, 2026) is $100 billion, indicating that forecasters are on track to significantly underestimate adoption.

We posed a similar question to our LEAP panel in summer 2026, asking them to predict the combined annualized revenue run rate of Anthropic and OpenAI at the end of 2026. Experts and superforecasters gave median forecasts of $70 billion and $90 billion, both of which are substantially below the likely current value for this question, $140 billion.17 Our LLM projection (as of August 18, 2026) estimates that this question will resolve at $165 billion, although this does not take into account the latest reporting on Anthropic’s revenue.

Although revenue projections seem on track to be very inaccurate, the picture for other AI-relevant economic indicators is more mixed. In the XPT, the median forecaster accurately predicted the lowest price of 1 GFLOPS by the end of 2024, and was reasonably close to predicting US computer R&D spending at the same resolution date.18

Broad adoption indicators: uncertain

In September–October 2025 we asked LEAP panelists to forecast the share of US work hours that would be assisted by generative AI in 2025. Experts and superforecasters gave median predictions of 4% and 3.6%, respectively, and the question resolved at 5.7%. However, in the question information we gave to forecasters we cited a historical baseline of 2% from an early version of a study from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. An update to this paper revised this value to 3.35%, so while the median forecasters appear to have underestimated here, it may be that they were mistakenly anchoring on out-of-date baseline information.

Resources relevant to AI growth: a mixed track record

A question we asked in the XPT in 2022 about the cost of the largest AI experiment run by the end of 2030 is also very likely to result in a dramatic underestimate from forecasters: expert and superforecaster median forecasts of $180 million and $100 million, respectively, have already been overtaken by Grok 4, which cost an estimated $388 million to train (published in mid-2025). Forecasts for the cost of the largest AI experiment before the end of 2024, however, were more mixed, with the experts predicting $65 million and superforecasters $35 million against a resolution of $45.8 million.

Forecasts about the resources related to AI growth appear to be on track to be much more accurate. In LEAP we’ve asked questions about the share of US electricity going toward AI, and the buildout of hyperscale data centers globally at various resolution dates. For the closer resolution dates, the majority of forecaster medians appear to be reasonably close to LLM projections (see table below).19

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!brGy!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F36a6f58c-e1f5-4c60-9307-17a9220c30de_1454x702.png]]

Table 2: Median expert and superforecaster predictions for the share of US electricity that will go toward AI training and deployment and total installed global capacity of hyperscale data centers.

Autonomous vehicles: experts overestimate adoption

We asked LEAP forecasters to predict the share of US ride-hailing trips that would be delivered by autonomous vehicles during 2027. The expert median for this question was 7.3%, which is on track to be a large overestimate compared to our LLM projection of 2.5%. Superforecasters appear to be notably more accurate on this question, giving a median prediction of 2%.

Future indicators

Many adoption forecasts from our studies have not yet resolved—for example, forecasts on drug discovery and diffusion across science. We’re also tracking forecasts on the share of US adults who self-report using AI for companionship daily by the end of 2027. The median expert and superforecaster both gave a forecast of 10%, which is above the LLM projection of 8% on this question.

Impacts

Our studies also capture a wide range of forecasts on AI’s impacts. These include impacts on employment and economic growth, but also AI’s effect on cybercrime, global catastrophic risk, and improving life expectancy. Not enough forecasts of this kind have resolved to draw any meaningful conclusions about accuracy, but we cover some preliminary data below.

Economic and labor impact

In the XPT we asked forecasters to predict the share of US GDP that would come from software and information services in 2024. They slightly overestimated this share, but their median forecasts were close to the resolution figure of 3.25%.20 In the same study, forecasters slightly underestimated the OECD labor force participation rate for 2024, but were again pretty close to the true resolution value.21

In LEAP, we’ve asked for forecasts on a range of economic and labor outcomes, including those in the table below. It is too early to assess the accuracy of these forecasts.

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!FBeA!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd534437f-13e1-4bd8-af3b-c5a1ee397bfb_1456x436.png]]

Table 3: Median expert and superforecaster predictions, and LLM projections of key economic outcomes in an unconditional scenario.

We also asked for many more macroeconomic forecasts in our study on the economic effects of AI.

Other impact measures

In the XPT, we asked forecasters to predict the share of Americans who would say they had a negative opinion of AI by the end of 2024. Here, the median expert and superforecaster predictions of 33% were extremely close to the resolution of 32.9%.

In our study on AI cyber risk we asked for the year in which an AI-enabled attacker causes a grid blackout causing $100 million or more in damages. Experts and superforecasters gave median predictions of 2031 and 2035, respectively, though this question is yet to resolve. In LEAP we asked for predictions of the annual losses from cybercrime reported to the FBI in 2026, 2028, and 2031, so we should have some resolution data on this question relatively soon.

In many of our studies we’ve elicited forecasts on catastrophic risk, AI-enabled pandemic risk, large-scale harm events, and other forms of major risk. We have also elicited forecasts on major potential benefits from AI such as improvements in life expectancy. These are some of the most important forecasts across our work, but it’s too early to say if high or low risk and benefit estimates are more accurate. For more information, see our LEAP waves on risks from AI and benefits from AI.

Geopolitics and governance

Although we only have a small number of questions in this category, it’s worth highlighting one recent question that appears to have surprised forecasters.

In LEAP Wave 9 (May–June 2026), we asked forecasters to predict the calendar year by which either the US, UK, or EU governments would issue a binding directive, regulation, court order, or injunction to delay, seriously restrict, or condition the public release of an AI system, based on safety risks. The median expert and superforecaster gave a 50% chance this would happen by 2030.

In fact, this question may be very close to resolution already. In late June, OpenAI restricted availability of its unreleased model GPT-5.6 Sol to a small group of partners approved by the US government. It is not clear that this meets our resolution criteria, as this does not appear to be the result of a binding directive, but this and the Claude Fable post-release restrictions suggest that resolution on this question is potentially much closer than forecasters anticipated.

Other unresolved geopolitics and governance questions include:

The share of frontier AI chips produced by the US, China, Taiwan, and other regions;

The year in which NATO or a member state will publicly authorize the use of fully autonomous offensive cyber operations or cyber weapons;

Whether a top-four frontier lab will exist within a non-democracy by 2030.

Limitations

This post is intended as a brief overview of where median AI progress forecasts appear to be inaccurate across our studies, but there are several major limitations to our approach and caveats worth bearing in mind, including:

Our methodology is biased toward identifying underestimates of AI progress as it is easier to identify forecasts where the current value has already overshot the median forecasters’ predictions. If an AI capability predicted to occur in 2030 is actually achieved in 2035, we will need to wait many years to report on this overestimation.22 The vast majority of our AI progress forecasts are unresolved and it may be the case that over time the picture of forecaster accuracy changes significantly.

In this post we have concentrated almost exclusively on median forecasts, which may obscure more accurate predictions from subsets of forecasters, as well as information from forecasts covering other percentiles.

In some cases, issues with our question specification or our elicitation format may have led to inaccurate forecasts. For example, for LiveCodeBench Pro (Hard) forecasts, it may be that some forecasters did not understand that the benchmark allows models to go back and test on questions from earlier quarters.23

Discussion

Overall, AI capabilities and some important measures of adoption (such as AI company revenue) are moving much faster than experts and superforecasters expected.

One potential implication of this is that forecasters should expect much faster AI progress, faster AI adoption, and much larger AI impacts going forward.

We have seen some evidence that forecasters in LEAP are updating in this direction. In summer 2025 and spring 2026, we asked panelists to forecast the likelihood of AI in 2040 reaching various levels of impact on the Technological Richter Scale (TRS, a scale devised by Nate Silver that ranks technologies by their broad societal impact). Over the course of nine months, experts and superforecasters have increased the likelihood they assign to AI’s impact being comparable to “technology of the millennium” (e.g., agriculture, Level 9), while continuing to assign the greatest probability to AI being comparable to “technology of the century” (e.g., electricity, Level 8):24

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!7iVC!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd03b11ca-8b67-4289-af0c-b624bff5e317_6800x7800.png]]

Figure 5: Wave 1 vs. Wave 8 TRS forecasts, matched participants only. The figure shows the mean probability assigned to each TRS level in Wave 1 and Wave 8, restricted to participants who completed both waves.

If forecasters are updating their views toward faster AI progress, we might expect them to perform more accurately on benchmark questions asked more recently. However, we have not yet seen evidence of improved accuracy on more recent questions. Forecasters likely majorly underestimated progress on the METR time horizon benchmark (asked in April 2026) and underestimated OpenAI and Anthropic revenue growth in our July 2026 survey. We will try to understand what is driving forecasters’ continued accuracy errors and will take various steps to highlight more accurate and relevant forecasts, which we’ll expand on in the next post in this series.

An alternative response to the evidence in this post is to say that benchmarks have moved much faster than forecasters expected in part because it was easier to “teach to the test” than forecasters expected and therefore that benchmarks are less meaningful for making sense of real-world AI capabilities than forecasters might have expected. Perhaps significant benchmark progress just doesn’t lead to real-world impacts in many areas. In which case, we might expect forecasters to underestimate AI progress on benchmarks, but turn out to be more accurate when it comes to forecasting real-world impacts such as macroeconomic impacts.

This debate highlights the importance of getting accuracy data on additional adoption and impact measures, which we expect to have soon as more questions resolve.

Next steps

In this post, we have covered the accuracy of median forecasts across our studies, often highlighting places where these median forecasts have been inaccurate. However, subsets of forecasters in our studies have been much more accurate than the median forecaster.

In the next post in this series, we’ll look at a few ways we can improve the accuracy and relevance of LEAP forecasts and highlight predictions from more accurate forecasters. These involve three core updates to LEAP:

Highlighting forecasts from a subsample of panelists who expect very fast AI progress by 2040.

Adding continuously updated LLM forecasts to LEAP findings.

Identifying our most accurate LEAP participants and highlighting their forecasts as soon as we have sufficient data to make this judgment.

1 Ezra Karger, Bridget Williams, and Simas Kučinskas also provided feedback on this post.

LLM forecasts have steadily improved in recent years, and ForecastBench indicates that some models now perform at superforecaster level on certain question types. GPT-5.5 with "high" reasoning currently leads the ForecastBench Tournament Leaderboard among models tested "out of the box" by FRI—that is, models without forecasting-specific scaffolding. Importantly, the projections we use in this post were elicited months after humans forecasted the same questions. Hence, these LLM projections can best be thought of as capable forecasters with a substantial comparative advantage from having seen more real-world development over recent months, rather than simply a comparison of LLM and human forecasts.

3Tom Cunningham summarized the broad range of disagreement about AI’s economic impacts in a post first published in November 2025.

Median forecasts for both groups were below the latest published value available at the time of forecasting. While one might hold the view that either or both companies’ revenue will collapse before year’s end, rationales showed no evidence that a large number of these forecasters intended to predict a reversal of recent trends.
