controls.title: AI Experts Largely Agree on Which Policies Most Reduce Catastrophic AI Risk
controls.full_text:
Summary

Over the last few months, AI risk has burst into the public and political consciousness in a big way. A combination of real cyber incidents, high-profile resignations, and statements from lab leaders has brought the discussion of catastrophic risk to a level of prominence that just a year ago seemed highly improbable.

While there are plenty of catastrophic risk estimates out there (including from our forecasters), we know much less about what people think about how policy can address risk from AI. Is AI risk addressable by policy? If so, which are the right policy levers to pull, and what is the likelihood of them being implemented?

The Longitudinal Expert AI Panel (LEAP) brings together forecasts from the kinds of experts that policymakers look to when considering the future of AI: computer scientists, AI industry experts, top economists, policy experts, and AI risk experts. In Wave 12 we asked our panelists to consider how far various policies would go toward addressing catastrophic risks from AI. We also asked panelists which policies they supported, and which ones they thought had the highest chances of being implemented.

We’ve also recruited a new expert sample, composed of people who work on addressing the risks posed by transformative AI. In this and subsequent work, we’ll report results from this “AI risk experts” group as well as our other experts, superforecasters, and our representative sample of the US general public.

The results from our policy forecasts are encouraging. LEAP panelists believe that specific policies can substantially reduce the risk of AI-caused catastrophes, and experts largely agree on which policies should be implemented, despite their disparate professional backgrounds and views on AI. Across groups, clear majorities support establishing an international body with pre-release authorization power over frontier models and expect doing so to have among the largest risk-reducing effects. Majorities of most groups also support policies to slow AI progress and strengthen AI labs’ liability for harms caused by their models, policies most forecasters also expect to meaningfully reduce risk.

However, when it came to implementing these policies, forecasters were much more pessimistic. The policies most expected to reduce risk were also the ones that respondents thought were least likely to be implemented. The one policy that was associated with an increase in risk—federal preemption of state AI laws—was seen as the most likely to pass. Panelists also noted throughout that although bilateral (US–China) versions of policies were more likely to reduce catastrophic risk from AI, they were also less likely to be implemented.

In essence, this wave highlights a contradiction at the heart of the AI policy debate. Forecasters believe that policy really can reduce risks from AI, but are pessimistic that governments will put in place the policies that have the highest impact.

Read on for more detailed insights from our wave of policy forecasts. You can also read the full report, with a question-by-question breakdown and forecaster rationales on the LEAP website.

Policies

We asked forecasters to consider the following policies:1

P1: Federal preemption of state AI laws

A US federal statute or action barring states from regulating AI more strictly than the federal government.

P2: AI capability slowdown

Unilateral decision by US policymakers or a bilateral/multilateral decision made jointly by policymakers in China and the United States to slow the development of frontier AI systems.

P2.a: US enacts a policy to slow AI development, with no qualifying measure binding the US and China in force.

P2.b: US and China agree to a single bilateral or multilateral measure to slow AI development.

P3: Pre-release authorization for frontier models

A binding requirement that frontier models be vetted and authorized before release, imposed by a US federal body or by an international body.

P3.a: A US federal body holds pre-release authorization power.

P3.b: An international body whose member jurisdictions include the US and China holds pre-release authorization power over frontier models.

P4: Strict liability

A US federal statute treating frontier model training and deployment as an abnormally dangerous activity subject to strict liability (i.e., a regime under which a developer is liable for harms its models cause without the injured party having to prove the developer was careless or the model defective).

P5: Bundle of policies (P2.b, P3.b, and P4)

Assume all three policies are in force: a binding US–China measure slowing frontier AI development, an international body (with member jurisdictions including the US and China) holding pre-release authorization power over frontier models, and federal strict liability for frontier AI harms.

Key insights

Respondents disagree significantly about how risky AI is, yet still largely agree on what to do about it

We started by asking forecasters to give us their baseline all-things-considered forecasts of the likelihood of an AI-caused catastrophe that leads to the deaths of more than 10% of humans by 2050. Here’s what they forecast:2

Experts: 2%

Superforecasters: 1.6%

AI risk experts: 5.2%

General public: 5%

As these forecasts show, there is wide disagreement about the baseline level of risk. AI risk experts give risk estimates that are more than double those of our general expert sample, and three times higher than superforecasters.

Despite this disagreement about the level of baseline risk, panelists largely agreed about which AI risk policies should be implemented. A majority of forecasters in each group agreed that the following four policies should be implemented:3

Pre-release authorization requirement (international body, including US and China)

Pre-release authorization requirement (US-only)

Strict liability for developers

AI capability slowdown (US–China)

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!J7lm!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc5d428ca-0a2b-4a03-ad5d-a43ac81184a0_2000x2120.png]]

The only policy that did not win majority support in any group of forecasters was a federal preemption of state AI laws. This was supported by just 29% of experts, 14% of superforecasters, 20% of AI risk experts, and 50% of the general public. The most divisive policy was a US-only capability slowdown—34% of experts and 35% of superforecasters thought this policy should be implemented, compared with 60% of AI risk experts and 65% of the general public.

Respondents across groups believe policy can substantially reduce catastrophic AI risk

After they gave us their baseline forecasts of AI-caused catastrophic risk, we asked forecasters to predict the same outcome but this time to assume that each of the policies described above was implemented immediately by the relevant governing body.

Experts forecast lower catastrophic risk under five of seven policies in our policy menu, indicating strong belief across forecasters that policies can address a substantial portion of AI-caused catastrophic risk.4 Experts and superforecasters expected an international pre-release authorization body for frontier models to be the most effective single policy at reducing risk, while AI risk experts predicted the largest effects from a US–China slowdown agreement.

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!YNOi!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F724c2583-d527-48ed-88ef-92a537259c9b_2000x2106.png]]

All groups expected large reductions in risk from an international pre-release regime or a US–China slowdown agreement, forecasting that both policies would reduce risk by between 20% and 50% compared with the baseline. The three-policy bundle of US–China capability slowdown, international pre-release authorization, and strict liability was associated with the largest decrease in risk of any policy we tested—a forecast 72% reduction in risk from experts, 62% reduction from AI risk experts and a 56% reduction from superforecasters.

Forecasters strongly support the implementation of an international body with pre-release authorization power over frontier models

All groups strongly supported a policy that would give an international body whose member jurisdictions include the US and China pre-release authorization power over frontier models. In terms of support for implementation, this was the most-favored policy by experts (75% in favor), superforecasters (86% in favor), and the general public (84% in favor). For AI risk experts this was the second-most-favored policy (86% in favor), narrowly behind a US–China capability slowdown, which 87% of that group favored.

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Jaww!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F02542dc0-1df5-4ca3-9cbe-4583a4884fdb_2000x1600.png]]

Forecasters also agreed that an international pre-release authorization regime would significantly reduce the risk of an AI-caused catastrophe by 2050. Compared with their baseline risk probabilities, forecasts of an AI-caused catastrophe fell by at least 23% when conditioned on implementation of this policy:

Experts: 2% → 1% (-50%)

Superforecasters: 1.6% → 1% (-38%)

AI risk experts: 5.2% → 4% (-23%)

General public: 5% → 3% (-40%)

For experts, superforecasters, and the general public, only the policy bundle was associated with a greater decrease in AI-caused catastrophic risk.

US-only policies are forecast to significantly reduce AI risk, but are still seen as less effective than bilateral policy

For two policies, we asked forecasters to predict the effect of a version implemented by the US only, and a version implemented bilaterally or multilaterally by the US and China. These were a decision by policymakers to slow the development of frontier AI systems (P2), and a binding requirement that frontier models be vetted and authorized before release, imposed by a US federal body or by an international body (P3).

The bilateral version of both of these policies was associated with a larger reduction in catastrophic risk compared with a US-only version of the policy. For example, experts gave a baseline 2% chance of an AI-caused catastrophe by 2050. This risk was unchanged if a US-only AI capability slowdown was implemented, and fell to 1.2% if this slowdown was implemented in both the US and China. For the pre-release authorization policy, the chance of an AI catastrophe fell to 1.5% (US-only version) and 1% (international version). This same pattern holds true across forecaster groups and when forecasters assess the chance of a smaller “sub-catastrophe,” which causes at least 1,000,000 deaths within a five-year period.

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fdNO!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8b0cbe5b-f04b-49ac-9b52-a2d6f4126906_2000x1550.png]]

Despite bilateral policies being viewed as the most impactful, forecasters thought they were less likely to be implemented when compared with US-only versions of the same policy. Experts assigned a 20% probability to a pre-release authorization policy being implemented in the US before the end of 2030, compared with a 5% chance of an international version of the policy being implemented by the same date. For the AI capability slowdown policy, experts gave an 8% chance of a US-only version being implemented and a 5% chance to a bilateral version being implemented.

Experts strongly oppose federal preemption and think its passage would increase AI risk. But they also think it's the policy most likely to pass

A federal preemption of state AI laws was the only policy associated with an increase the risk of an AI-caused catastrophe by 2050 by all forecaster groups. These are the median forecasts of each group in the unconditional scenario, and then conditional on a federal preemption of state AI laws being passed, with the increase in risk in such a scenario shown in brackets:

Experts: 2% → 3% (+50%)

Superforecasters: 1.6% → 2.5% (+56%)

AI risk experts: 5.2% → 8% (+54%)

General public: 5% → 6.9% (+38%)

Federal preemption also had the lowest support for implementation of any of the policies we tested. Just 29% of experts supported implementation, with 14% of superforecasters, 20% of AI risk experts, and 50% of the general public in support. Despite this, experts assigned this policy the highest likelihood of passing—forecasting a 26% chance that such a policy is implemented by the end of 2030, rising to 40% by the end of 2050. This policy was also forecast as the most likely to pass by 2030 by the general public, with superforecasters and AI risk experts placing slightly more likelihood on pre-release authorization (US only) being implemented by 2030.

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!KJkH!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffa6ff3e0-be6d-441b-b378-abe48c399864_2000x1520.png]]

In their rationales, forecasters noted that companies often choose to comply with the strictest state standard, setting a national "floor" for safety standards, which a federal preemption would remove. Several forecasters argued that preemption's impact on catastrophic risk would be minimal, as much of the state-level regulation that might be preempted was unlikely to focus on catastrophic risk, and instead would address other concerns such as discrimination, bias, data exploitation, and so on.

The policies expected to reduce risk the most are those respondents think least likely to be implemented

We asked forecasters to predict the probability that the relevant governing body/bodies will implement each policy by the end of 2030 and 2050. Across all groups, most respondents place the probability of implementation by the end of 2030 at or below 25% for almost all policies.

Experts predict the largest reductions in risk under international pre-release approval, US–China slowdown, and strict liability. They also think these policies are least likely to be implemented, giving all three a 5% chance of being in place by 2030.

Conversely, experts give the highest chance of implementation to federal preemption (26%), under which they expect risk to increase.

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!sdWo!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2dfefcde-41e1-41e0-987f-2b01c6b1bb75_2000x1660.png]]

Despite placing a high probability of implementation of federal preemption and US pre-release authorization, forecasters expect these policies to be among the least effective at reducing catastrophic AI risk. In contrast, the bundle of three policies, which is ranked as the most effective at reducing catastrophic AI risk compared to the baseline by all groups, is seen as the least likely to be implemented. For instance, experts expect the bundle of policies to reduce catastrophic AI risk by nearly 72%, but give only a 1% chance of these policies being implemented. This trend is seen across other policies where forecasters predict catastrophic AI risk will be lowered, including capability slowdowns (P2), pre-release authorization, and strict liability (P4).

Comparing EA-affiliated forecasters with other forecasters

Recent discourse about AI risk has focused on effective altruism (EA) and the differences in beliefs between EA-influenced individuals and other groups. We anticipated this discussion when designing LEAP, and we can explore this dynamic in our LEAP sample by splitting respondents into two groups:

1) Experts with connections to EA, including grant recipients and employees of EA-adjacent organizations, based on our sample definition last year5

2) Experts with no connection to EA

The figure below shows that these two groups hold virtually identical preferences about which policies they think should be implemented and have directionally similar beliefs about the impact of policies on catastrophic risk.

In other words, our headline results are not driven by experts connected to effective altruism. Instead, they represent a broadly shared view of a representative sample of experts.

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!hbsi!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb8ed3b3f-bd36-4e12-8744-1190bfe9b31e_2000x1600.png]]

Find out more

For full results from Wave 12, visit the LEAP website.

1This list covers several options that are currently prominent in the discourse, but is certainly non-exhaustive. Among other things, it does not cover policies aimed at improving societal resilience or response to catastrophe. Future LEAP waves will likely address other types of policy that could not fit into this wave’s survey.

2Note that “baseline” refers to forecasters' median unconditional forecasts (their all-things-considered predictions that include what policies they expect to be implemented). We also had forecasters predict risk under a strong “status quo” assumption of no meaningful policy change. These estimates are uniformly higher, implying that all groups expect some effective policy to be implemented.

3It is possible that forecasters were primed to be more likely to support these policies by their inclusion in a survey focused on risk. We did ask forecasters to consider and name tradeoffs that apply to these policies, but the balance of our questions focused on risk, making a priming effect plausible.

4In this report we compare median forecasts under different conditions as our main analysis of the effects of those conditions. For example, we compare the median risk prediction across experts under international pre-release restrictions to the median risk prediction across experts under the unconditional scenario to estimate the effect of international pre-release restrictions according to experts. We could also use the median individual’s difference in risk between the two conditions to answer the same question. The specific numbers sometimes change under this alternative method, but not the overall takeaways presented here.

5 See the LEAP launch paper for the full definition of our EA-affiliated group

controls.title: Game Design Creativity evals
controls.full_text:
A personal eval I run on new AI models is “design a novel game, with mechanics that have never been seen before.” I do this because this is a domain I have enough taste in that I think I can tell if they are doing something actually creatively interesting. [1]

For a long time, they would always say “time manipulation mechanics!” as their first answer. Braid was cool, guys, but, it's almost 20 years old now.

But reasoning models started getting novel. Later models started getting reasonably fun.

o1

OpenAI's o1 started to impress me. It came up with:

Scratch and sniff board game, where what cards smell like determine what powers they have.

Okay I'm not sure what that means and it's not obviously functionally different from regular vision-based cards. I think the implementation details it gave didn't actually do much that a regular board game with the powers written down normally would have.  When I thought about it myself I did come up with some things you might do with it.

But, I sure have never heard of a scratch and sniff boardgame.

Opus 4.6

I gave Opus 4.6 a prompt beginning with "Generate a game design that prominently features a novel _concept_, not just a novel mechanic."

Opus 4.6 gave me this overly meta but, AFAICT, pretty original game concept. (I don't think it actually featured "a novel concept" in the way I meant, still felt like it had done something notable).

In every game ever designed, the rules exist before play begins. Even in rule-changing games (Nomic, Fluxx, Calvinball), rule modifications apply going forward.

Tabula Rasa inverts this. You place pieces first, in a meaning-vacuum. Then, in alternating phases, you define what the pieces mean — and those definitions apply retroactively to everything already on the board.

The actual implementation is less exciting than the initial pitch – it doesn't include defining rules that govern causality within the game universe.

I was intrigued reading it to imagine a game where part of what you're doing is reverse-building-a-jenga-tower-of-rules, where initially there's a lot of degrees of freedom of what rules to insert but you become more constrained.

Instead, the rules here just determine what various pieces are worth. Players take turns placing pieces in various configurations, and playing rule cards that establish "this sort of pattern is worth this many points." Which is not really that different from many other board games.

But, fwiw here's part of its explanation:

What Makes It Strategically Deep

Hedging: Early in the game, you build many simultaneous patterns, because you don't know which patterns will become valuable. A diagonal of your tokens is meaningless until someone defines "diagonal-of-3 same-color → +5 points."

Counter-definition: You see your opponent building clusters? Define a rule that makes clusters of their color lose points. But now you've used one of your 3 rule slots on offense rather than building your own scoring engine.

Trap patterns: Build something that looks like you want diagonal-scoring... but actually you want your opponent to waste a counter-definition on it, while your real plan relies on adjacency patterns.

Temporal tension: Define scoring rules early (locking in points but giving your opponent many turns to play around them)? Or late (surprising your opponent but having fewer pieces left to place)?

Prompt leading to Tabula Rasa

Generate a game design that prominently features a novel _concept_, not just a novel mechanic. This is a test of your creativity. We're seeing if you have the ability to form new building block concepts that are practically useful. Game design is a specialty of mine, so I can evaluate whether you've done novel conceptual thinking.

Creative Concepts?

There's some question of "how innovative really, is that?"

It was pretty obvious that LLMs would eventually be able to encyclopedically look at every human concept or mechanic and search for ones that meet various game design constraints with brute force.

In the Opus 4.6 challenge, I asked for a novel concept – not just a new mechanic. It didn't really understand the assignment. To be honest, I'm not 100% sure what the assignment was exactly. What we actually care about is "if an AI is solving a problem, and has a conceptual hole that no human has written down anywhere, will it notice, and be able to invent a new concept from scratch?" And "make a game with a novel concept" is more like a weird fake assignment than an attempt at that.

I think the missing-piece of AGI is something like "sufficiently good taste in what counts as a useful concept when the problem isn't well defined." But, I'm wasn't sure how to operationalize that at the time, or, at the time I wrote most of this blogpost (this week).

Each concept should be interesting enough to inspire one major thread of the game that is fun and interesting in isolation, and they should combine together in a way that feels like an emergent 3rd concept.

Take as long as you need to figure out how to find novel concepts.

Also make sure it has innovative, beautiful graphics of a type never seen before.

Runners, shuttles and timed gates only move in real time while you could still get in their way. Once you can’t, they finish instantly. A runner you can’t catch is already in its pit, however far it had to go. A shuttle you can never reach is smeared along its whole rail, and it settles into one position once you can reach it. The past doesn’t end at a moment; it ends at the edge of your reach. The levels make you think like this:

You can’t outrun what you can’t stop. If a runner you can’t catch is going to lock a door, that door is locked now.

To make something happen sooner, make yourself unable to stop it, for example by stepping through a one-way door.

To pin down something that is everywhere at once, make yourself able to touch it.

B. Needed: “Nothing exists that makes no difference.”
A frost wall exists only if some eye in the level would see differently without it. You can’t break a wall, but you can make it pointless by giving its job to a crate or your own shadow. A dotted outline marks a wall that will appear the moment it has a job.

C. Permission, which comes out of A and B together: “A change may reach the eyes only while you could still stop it.”

If a runner becomes unstoppable and would change what an eye sees, a wall appears in its path and stops it. A runner you could still stop rolls straight through that spot. So if you let go, the world stops it for you; if you stay close, it gets through.

Some walls touch no light at all. They exist only to keep you away from a smeared shuttle, so they protect the very fate that makes them necessary. They open exactly at the moments when your arriving would change nothing.

Graphics. The board draws its own reasons:

Cells you can reach are tinted cool, as the open present. Everything else is hatched in sepia, as already past.

Gold light is what the eyes actually see. Dashed cyan light is what a wall is holding back, with a thread to the eye it serves.

Things that finish instantly leave trails like Marey’s motion photographs, and smears are drawn as long exposures.

The drawing techniques themselves are ordinary; what’s new is what they show.

My guess at your verdict

Already: about 50%. The old idea is that the past can’t be prevented (Ockham called it “accidental necessity”). Already turns it around and makes it a law of time, and I found no earlier use of that. But it echoes things you know well: light cones, precommitment and burning bridges, and, for the smear, quantum superposition and Outer Wilds’ quantum objects. I don’t think any of those makes “I can’t stop it” the reason something is already done. Still, after thinking about it you may file it as “light cone plus commitment”.

Needed: about 25%. I expect you’ll see it as “Making Beliefs Pay Rent” applied to walls, or as the Eleatic principle or the legal but-for test. What’s new is that existence can be passed from one object to another, but the slogan itself is old.

Both: about 15%. “Already but not Needed” and “neither” seem about equally likely. If you grade Permission too, I expect it to do best of the three, since I found nothing like a wall that exists to protect a fate.

Claude:

The closest match to that exact framing is Raymond Arnold (“Raemon”) on LessWrong. His 2023 post “Feedbackloop-first Rationality” argues that the core skill is inventing feedback loops for fuzzy, hard-to-measure problems, rather than only practicing where feedback already exists. He has since built workshops and a series of posts around that idea, often with exercises like puzzle games used as training grounds for strategy. If you want the concept almost word for word, start there.

Other people who circle the same idea from different angles:

Cedric Chin (Commonplace) writes about how experts actually learn in messy real-world domains. He covers tacit knowledge, the limits of deliberate practice outside sports and music, and Naturalistic Decision Making.

Gary Klein is the researcher behind much of what Chin draws on. His work covers how experts build intuition through recognition and feedback in the field.

Logan Strohl developed “naturalism,” a method for noticing subtle, previously invisible signals in your own experience. In practice that means building new feedback channels where none seemed to exist.

Andy Matuschak and Michael Nielsen write about building tools and practices that tighten learning loops, especially around memory and understanding.

Scott Young (Ultralearning) treats feedback as a core principle. That includes finding or creating feedback when a skill doesn’t naturally give it.

John Boyd’s OODA loop and Eric Ries’s build-measure-learn loop are the older, more formalized ancestors. They’re more about running a known loop fast than inventing new ones on the fly.

If you’re specifically interested in the meta-skill of finding new loops, as opposed to iterating quickly inside existing ones, Raemon and Strohl are the most direct, with Chin and Klein as the evidence base.

Okay, game concept: Fluidtorio

You are building a series of factory colonies that float in different types of fluid. You build little modules that need to stay afloat, but, also accomplish various other goals (i.e. be a factory that processes some materials that you need to build other tools to build more modules to advance to new zones with different fluids to contend with).

Your town floats on a layer of ~oil over a layer of ~water (or equivalent), and above you are a few layers of atmosphere that do different things. Ascending up and down is part of the game.

The actual materials – both the fluids, and the stuff you need to build around them, are procedurally generated each game, so you don't know exactly how they interact.

Things are setup such that you will eventually need to build relatively large, dense towers to accomplish stuff, and somehow thread the needle on "stay afloat, while doing complex engineering challengers." Kinda factorio style.

If you naively build towards your goal, your towers are going to collapse.

You are on a time limit before a volcano explodes or something. You do not, by default, have enough time to brute force trying the different combinations to escape the planet. So, a central challenge is figuring out how to rapidly test materials to figure out what your limitations are, and then planning what series of things to build to bootstrap to the rocket age in time.

This includes buoyancy/weight/factory-processing-output-balancing stuff, where your towers and stockpiles might collapse. There also needs to be some kind of crafting system where stuff explodes or doesn't work right, in a way that is reasonably procedural so it's different each time but has enough structure to reliably make sense and be fun and feel tactile.

There can also be feedback-loops vis-a-vis "where to explore to find resources."

That's how far I got before running out of timebox. Okay. Making that seems nontrival, but, that feels like a fair benchmark to hold an AI against.

I followed up with the first AI, asking some questions about the assignment. You can read it's answers in detail...

What do you think "a concept" is, in this context?

Here’s how I’d define a concept, and how my results measure against it.

My working definition. A concept is a reusable unit of thought: a way of carving up situations that lets you see new cases as instances of it and draw inferences you couldn’t easily draw before. A good one has three properties:

It transfers. Once you have it, you notice it in places it wasn’t built for. “Goodhart’s law”, “Schelling point” and “opportunity cost” work this way.

It licenses new moves. It changes what feels like the obvious next step, not just what you know.

It holds more than its definition. Working it through gives you consequences you didn’t put in.

How it differs from nearby things:

A mechanic is a rule inside one system. It can be new without changing how you think anywhere else.

A combination joins two concepts, “X but with Y”. It’s new as a pairing, but you could think it with what you already had.

A premise like “imagine a world where Z” is a proposition. It only becomes a concept if Z gives you a lens you keep using.

What I actually optimized for. The prompts I wrote for the helpers turned “concept” into roughly “a new kind of world-law that forces a new mental operation.” That’s narrower than the definition above, and it steered the search toward strange physics. Judged by the stricter definition:

Already and Needed are mostly premises. Their parent ideas, unpreventability and but-for necessity, are old. What’s new is the moves they force: “make yourself unable to stop it so it happens now,” and “to remove a wall, give its job to something else.” Those moves are vivid inside the game. I’m less sure they transfer outside it.

The self-justifying wall comes closest to a real concept. It’s a structure that exists because it stops you from changing the fate that makes it necessary,

What would dramatic success look like?

For this challenge, I’d say dramatic success is a concept that outlives the game. People keep using it after they forget the puzzles, because it names something real they couldn’t think about cleanly before.

What you’d observe:

It becomes vocabulary. Months later, you or a commenter use it in an argument that has nothing to do with games, and it does work there.

It explains real cases. You start noticing instances: institutions, codebases, relationships, physical systems. The concept predicts something about them that you wouldn’t have predicted otherwise.

Experts don’t have it. A philosopher of causation, a game designer and a mathematician each look and say “we don’t have a name or a theory for this”, and they still say it after a serious search.

The game is the best way to learn it. Playing builds an intuition that reading the definition doesn’t. “Rules are objects you can push” felt like nothing until Baba Is You made it physical.

Other people build with it. It becomes a building block: other designers make levels or games from it, or a theorist formalizes it.

Historical concepts at that level: the tragedy of the commons, Schelling points, Goodhart’s law. In games, Portal’s “speedy thing goes in, speedy thing comes out” and Baba’s rules as objects changed how a generation of players and designers think about puzzle space.

Against that bar, my result:

Already probably fails test 1. “Make yourself unable to stop it so it happens now” is vivid in the game, but I’m not sure it names anything outside it that “precommitment” doesn’t already cover.

Needed fails test 3. Philosophers would recognize it.

The self-justifying wall is the only part that might pass test 2. Real structures do persist because they stop anyone from creating the situation that would make them unnecessary. But it would need to beat “entrenchment” and “regulatory capture” on test 3, and I doubt it does by much.

So my honest expectation is modest success: novel as a game, maybe a borderline concept. Dramatic success would look like you, unprompted, calling something on LessWrong a “guardian wall” six months from now, with that being the clearest way to say it.

Do you have thoughts on what you could have done differently? (looking at the earliest committed notes?)

Reading brainstorm-prompts.md and selection-notes.md again, most of what I’d change was decided in the first prompt I wrote. The search was set up to find strange new physics for a puzzle game, not new concepts.

1. I put the game into the concept search too early. Every agent ranked its ideas by “novelty × fun × playability in a 2D browser puzzle game.” That rewards ideas that make good mechanics, not ideas that change how you think. A better order: first find concepts that pass a transfer test (does it explain real cases outside games?), then ask which ones can become a game.

2. My definition of “concept” was too narrow. Five of the eight strategies asked for new entities, laws, minds, formal structures, or ways of depicting the world. So most of the output was new physics. Only two strategies, unnamed real patterns and craft transplants, looked at how the real world works. Those two produced the ideas closest to real concepts: Earned Selfhood, and the “frozen indexicals” idea (names like “New College” that outlive the frame they were coined in). I gave both of them less weight.

3. My novelty test favored obscurity over insight. I told the agents to “assume anything resembling a known idea will be called out.” I also gave them a long list of known ideas to avoid, and had them search “the idea + game”. That rewards ideas you can’t easily find, not ideas that are true and useful. “No game does this” is weak evidence of a new concept. A better test asks whether experts in the nearest field, such as philosophy of causation or economics, already have a name for it.

4. I misread a correlated signal as evidence. At 21:34 I wrote that five agents had “independently” reached counterfactual physics, and took that as a sign the area was under-explored. But they were all the same model given the same framing. Convergence is more likely a shared attractor, a place this model drifts toward by default. It may even mean the area is over-explored by models like me.

5. Timing and momentum shaped the choice. I was prototyping Fatefall within ten minutes of it arriving, and I decided at 21:46, two minutes before my note confirming the last report. The first idea that got built gained momentum. Fairer: wait for all eight reports, then prototype the top three or four briefly before choosing.

6. I chose for combinability over substance. My main reason for the pair was that it produced an emergent third concept. That is what you asked for. But it ranks two decent ideas that combine well above one strong idea that doesn’t.

7. I didn’t ask what counts as a concept. Your draft says you’re “not 100% sure what the assignment was”. One short question at the start, something like “a lens that transfers, or a weird premise that’s fun to inhabit?”, would have changed the whole search.

8. My early thinking left no trace. The first 37 minutes produced the framing that mattered most, and none of it is readable. Writing short notes to a file as I went would make the process inspectable, which matters for an eval like yours.

If I reran it, I’d ask for real but unnamed patterns, test them against real cases and against experts in the nearest field, and only then design a game around the one or two that survive.

...but in summary it said:

A concept is a reusable unit of thought: a way of carving up situations that lets you see new cases as instances of it and draw inferences you couldn’t easily draw before. A good one has three properties: it transfers, it licenses new moves, and it holds more than it's definition.

Dramatic success is a concept that outlives the game. People keep using it after they forget the puzzles, because it names something real they couldn’t think about cleanly before. It becomes vocabulary.

Experts wouldn't have it yet. The game would be the best way to learn it. Other people would go on to build with it.

I focused on a narrow definition of concept and started probing

I asked it to write up a brief for another AI to try again. I ended up editing to brief to emphasize "also, please make it fun." Another AI thought for awhile, and ended up with:

The concepts. Fourteen research helpers, each given one narrow domain (law, insurance, crafts, medicine, markets and so on), looked at about 560 candidate structures. About 535 turned out to be already named somewhere. I ranked the survivors on the four tests before I looked at any game-design material.

Fold-back signal: some warning signals are produced by the very thing whose failure they report, so they go quiet at the worst moment. Examples: the “silent chest” in severe asthma, Air France 447’s stall warning (silent deep in the stall, sounding again on the correct recovery input), and Hurricane Maria’s death count. My guess at novelty: 35–45%. The likely objection is “the hook effect, generalized”, or “Dunning–Kruger for instruments”.

Refractory-check capture: when passing a check buys immunity from the next one, the checked party gains by calling the check itself. Examples: John Major’s 1995 “put up or shut up” contest, the Conservative Party’s 12-month immunity rule, Whole Foods’ 2014 proxy manoeuvre, the 1921 Leipzig trials. Novelty: 40–50%.

Emergent, certified collapse: a check that reads a fold-back signal is easiest to pass past the fold, so the collapsing system gets certified and sealed off from help. A quiet target volunteering for inspection is a symptom. Examples: Mid Staffordshire gaining foundation-trust status mid-scandal, and Wirecard. Novelty: 30–40%.

I'm... not 100% sure if those concepts make sense or carve reality in a useful way. And, rather than "invent a new concept from scratch" it tried more for "find existing unnamed phenomena that are worth having a name for."

This isn't as potent as the cognitive work I was looking for. But it feels at least related? I feel like it at least did a pretty decent pass at the assignment I actually gave it.

Fold-back signal is a mediocre name but seems like a decent concept to want a handle for. (Another Claude-instance said there isn't a canonical name that covers all three examples, although different fields have some names it as applied to their field and gave it "15-25% novelty". The other Claude-instance also listed "foldback signal" as one suggested name, although also suggested "self-silencing alarm" which is way more intuitive to me.)

I found it's next actual game a bit confusing and un-fun.

I told it "Also, alas, this game is neither fun nor comprehensible, please try again with the game design part", and gave it a third try.

I found it's third game comprehensible, not super fun but at least I understood roughly where it was going for and could imagine it being fun-ish if tuned.

Do they understand "fun?"

Opus 5.5 is not near "top expert level" at Game Design. I'd say it's got, like, the taste of a high school kid just getting started coding some games, who's read some Mark Rosewater essays and has the gist of how to make a game. Or, I guess more realistically, it's like if Twilight Sparkle or Hermione read up everything there is to know about "fun" overnight and then made a game, and, like, Twilight Sparkle and Hermione are quite competent. Twilight Sparkle can throw a sleepover on her first try and it's not perfect but it's way better than you might have expected.

It does feel like it has all the pieces it needs, to get better at taste with straightforward within-paradigm scaling. Probably OpenAI/Anthropic's current secret frontier AI models are able to make a medium complexity game with some interesting taste/tactics on their first try, even if they are still missing some subtleties of "fun."

AIs I've talked to definitely understand fun in a pretty rich way, as you'd expect of Twilight Sparkle after she reads up on it. I asked Fable once to formalize fun and try to make a genetic algorithm for making a "fun" world to walk around it. On one hand, it didn't work, and failed in some weirdly dumb ways. But, it's initial responses were like [me paraphrasing from memory, aggregating some things that had a bit of prodding from me in between]

"Fun? That hasn't been exactly formalized already but probably what you want is one of the ways to formalize compression [link to some math theorem guy I whose name I forgot], and what a fun game is is a presentation of patterns that you keep needing to compress so you can think about them. You want something not too easy or hard to compress. When you run out of stuff to compress, the fun ends.

A naive failure mode would be "random noise that constantly slightly changes such that you never can fully compress it." Obviously you don't want that, so you want [some technique I forgot].

You also want a small meaningful set of choices at any given time (like 2-5), where the action space is comprehensible enough you can infer some consequences, but still be surprised by the outcome.

And I'm like... okay yep I think that is approximately what fun is.

They seem like Mary from Mary's Room, who knows all the neuroscience and color theory necessary to tell you anything you could possibly want to know about the color red, but has never actually seen the color red.

I didn't successfully get it to build a good walking simulator before I gave up and moved on, but I think if I gave Opus 5.5 more compute it might work (I've since set up a Modal account, so the genetic algorithm it was trying could actually scale sufficiently).

I do bet Fable 6 will be able to do it pretty fine.

⚖ Fable 6 [or obviously equivalent thing] will be able to 1-3 shot a procedurally generated walking simulator that makes something interesting and delightful to me using what seems like a reasonably operationalized metric of Fun. 63%

Can they manipulate and derive novel concepts?

It's not very hard to get AIs to generate ideas. It's hard to get them to generate new interesting ideas. The main thing I think AIs are missing is taste in what concepts and tools are appropriate, when they are in uncharted territory.

They didn't demonstrate being better at that in any general kind of way during my explorations last week. But, a specific skill I hadn't thought to ask about, which it does seem like they have, is:

"Probe the breadth of human knowledge, looking not merely for existing concepts, but for commonalities that might warrant having a new concept-handle."

I expect, when offscript on openended problems, they won't be very good at finding new concept-handles that actually help them. But, when I imagine a 10,000-thread swarm solving Millenium problems, it does seem like "probe the concept-space and see if any of it feels helpful to crystallize into a new concept, and see if that concept helps" is the sorta thing they outta be able to do?

Another thing they are missing is "Gain new system 1 intuitions on the fly, in the middle of solving a problem, so you can apply them much more efficiently." I'm kinda confused about the limits of continual learning, but, "spin up a copy of the latest open weight model and fine-tune it on a concept-handle you just came up with by brute force and then assign that model work" seems like the sorta thing they outta be able to do.

Generalized Taste

What has confused me for the past two years is... it really feels viscerally obvious to me that generalized "keep track of all your goals, and evaluate whether you have everything you need to succeed at your goal, and relentlessly probe for alternative frames and evaluate each of those too", is not that different-in-kind from the sort of stuff AIs are already able to do.

But, my intuitions predicted they would already be able to do that, and it seems like they keep getting really confused when going off-script in a way that seems like they don't got it yet.

But, like, we've clearly seen Claude be able to apply good software architectural taste, that it doesn't bother to apply when it gets down to actually build things. We've also seen it get better at overall architectural taste when building things over time.

Opus 5.5 clearly knew what a concept was and what the assignment was when I asked it directly.

I still bet on LLMs eventually discover generalized "ask themselves the obvious fucking question and then do the obvious fucking thing", probably sometime in the next year. But I am less confident about it than I would have been two years ago. I don't know if that's all you need for ASI, but, I'd bet we see a step-change when they do.

(I observe that OpenAI employees seem freaked out about AI capabilities having spiked rather suddenly, and it's plausible that the Highly Persistent Internal Model and/or Mythos 6 already have it)

^In the life before I was a rationalist, my primary identity was being a game designer. (Obviously you can be both, in practice I ended up with different interests once getting into rationality)

I aspired to become a professional, and did not. But, some cred: during the first Magic the Gathering Great Designer Search, of 1000 applicants, I made it into the top 64.

^Coming up with "s-factor" felt like one of the rare times during the Feedbackloop Rationality where I did some cognitive labor that didn't feel like just mechanically combining deas.

controls.title: What will happen to Indian IT?
controls.full_text:
[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!X7fy!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1f3dee7c-91dc-4bcd-b2b9-59be63cdb76f_2000x401.png]]

This article originally appeared in Issue 15: Work. Subscribe to the print magazine to get future issues delivered to your door.

The situation of the world is as such: Some countries are rich and other countries are poor. Being poor is quite unpleasant, and creates all sorts of problems; in general, it’s much more pleasant to be rich. (This is true of individuals just as it is of countries.) So countries that are poor will generally want to find ways in which they can become rich. The main way to do this, in this world of ours where some countries are much richer than others, is to sell things to the countries that are richer than you are.

So what do you sell?

The most straightforward thing to sell is simply what your land naturally produces — crops, or oil, or copper, or diamonds. Sometimes this works very well: There are a few cases where natural resources have made countries exceptionally rich. But usually it doesn’t work. Sometimes this is because most natural commodities (like, say, cocoa) just aren’t very scarce. And when natural resources are scarce, they bring with them all sorts of problems: overvalued currencies, corruption, weak institutions. There’s a reason the “resource curse” is such a famous concept. And even if you wanted to sell those resources, you’d still need to have them in the first place. A lot of countries don’t.

So selling natural resources usually isn’t a great bet. What about selling goods that you manufacture? There are quite a few countries that got rich doing that. You start out with a lot of cheap labor; you build a labor-intensive manufacturing sector, producing things like garments or circuit boards; and you gradually move up the value chain into more difficult and valuable things. This takes a long time, and requires a very difficult alignment of institutions and culture and circumstances, but when it works the results can be pretty extraordinary.

But it’s also very hard. Most poor countries have tried to become manufacturing powers over the last few decades; very few of them have succeeded. And there’s good evidence to suggest that it’s become much more difficult over the last few decades. As technology improves, labor-intensive manufacturing just isn’t as labor-intensive as it used to be: Manufacturing employment in most developing countries is lower than it was a few decades ago.

So resource-led growth is usually a bad strategy; manufacturing-led growth is very difficult. What do you do then?

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!k6Yy!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F37c9eba9-baff-4f46-8652-c2dc9267038c_2000x1667.png]]

Diego Mallo

In the last few decades, a new path has become possible: services-led growth. The resource strategy sells raw goods; the manufacturing strategy combines those raw goods with human labor and sells the finished result; the services strategy simply sells the labor.

This wasn’t really possible, of course, before the internet. People worked where they lived and tended to produce things where they worked: It wasn’t feasible for someone living in Argentina to have much of a relationship with a firm in California. People might migrate for work and send money back home — in the early twentieth century, there were certain Irish towns where the majority of the income came from those who had migrated to the United States — but “remote work” wasn’t really a thing, and selling labor wasn’t really a strategy for economic development.

The internet changed that. All sorts of labor that once had to be performed in one place could now be performed anywhere. Not all jobs, of course: mechanics, appraisers, and police officers would still have to be based at home. But if you ran a software company, you could employ engineers in any part of the world with a sufficiently fast internet connection, and pay those workers a fraction of what their American or European counterparts might make. The same with customer service jobs and back-office functions in general. And so from 1990 onwards, there was a veritable explosion of “outsourcing” and “offshoring.”

There were a lot of people who complained about this, of course: Outsourcing wasn’t a great deal for American or European workers. But it was a great deal for a lot of people in poorer countries: Wages that were a fraction of American pay were still, by local standards, very good money. And the greatest beneficiary of all of this — the country that bet the most heavily of all on services exports — was India.

India is a massive country; and for a long time it was very poor. Unlike other once-very-poor countries in Asia, like China or South Korea, India never managed to develop a competitive manufacturing sector: Its share of global manufacturing exports today is about the same as Vietnam’s, despite having 14 times Vietnam’s population. But over the last few decades, India has managed to build a competitive service sector. As the largest exporter of IT and BPO services in the world, India was “the world’s back office.”

India’s services export industry employs only a small share of the population: Perhaps five million people in a country of 1.5 billion. But IT is still crucial to the Indian economy. It accounts for roughly seven percent of GDP and about a quarter of India’s total exports; the consumption of its high-earning workers sustains a much larger ecosystem of domestic employment; and the services trade surplus it generates, about $190 billion in fiscal year 2025, substantially offsets India’s persistent goods trade deficit, which would otherwise pose severe balance-of-payments problems. Service exports are the primary mechanism by which tens of millions of Indians have entered the global middle class.

The question now, though, is how long the Indian services export model has left to survive.

For decades, Indian IT and BPO prospered because of a very particular arbitrage: Western firms could hire Indian workers, so that Western firms would save money and Indian workers would earn high local wages. But now there’s something that can underprice even the workers of Hyderabad and Chennai. AI models are very good and, for the quality of work they’re able to do, very cheap: They can’t do physical work (yet!), but neither can Indian employees who do their work remotely. Western firms hired Indian workers because they provided lots of value for the cost: AI, it seems, could provide even more value, for even less cost.

So it wasn’t too long after the AI boom of the last few years started that people started to suggest the first victims of displacement would be the IT and BPO workers of India. Daniel Gross, an influential tech investor, suggested in January 2024 that “$250b of India’s GDP exports are essentially GPT-4 tokens … what happens now?”

Gross was being provocative; we now look back with some condescension on the now-obvious limitations of GPT-4 and models like it. But his underlying logic was serious. The Indian IT and BPO sector had been built on a simple proposition: Indian labor was cheap, English-speaking, and technically competent, and Western firms were willing to pay for it. AI seems to break that model entirely. In a world where AI models can write code, answer calls, and process insurance claims faster and cheaper than humans, what happens to the services export path? We can get more specific. The models are already capable of doing those things. So: What happens now?

India, the world’s back office

As with all complex things, it’s hard to trace a single point of origin for the Indian IT sector. One could go back to the Nehruvian elite’s fostering of elite Indian technical education in the 1950s, or — if you wanted to be truly exacting — to the British imposition of English-language education in the 1830s. But the best place to start is with a disastrous policy decision in 1978.

For many decades after its independence, the Indian state was deeply distrustful of foreign investment, viewing it as a legacy of colonial exploitation and a threat to self-reliance. And so in 1973, the Indian government passed the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, which mandated that no foreign entity could own more than 40 percent of an Indian company. This was bad news for multinationals generally, and eventually resulted in Coca-Cola leaving the Indian market and not returning until 1993; but it was particularly bad news for IBM, which was then the largest technology company in the world and by far the dominant player in the Indian computing market. IBM simply refused to dilute its stake in its Indian subsidiary. Discussions dragged on for several years, until a trade unionist named George Fernandes became the country’s Minister for Industries. Fernandes had led anti-computer protests in Bombay in the 1960s; and once in power he took a hard line against IBM. In June 1978, IBM abandoned the Indian market. About 800 IBM installations — large, bulky mainframes — were left stranded.

This was, it turned out, a perfect catalyst for the emergence of a domestic IT sector.

At the time, there wasn’t much of a computing industry in India. The Tata Group, India’s largest company, had a fledgling IT business called Tata Consulting Services; and there was a tiny computing startup called Hindustan Computers Limited, which was focused on building minicomputers for the Indian market. To fill the vacuum left by IBM, a few new players emerged. The Indian government created one company, the Computer Maintenance Corporation, to manage the abandoned IBM installations; and in the 1980s two new startups — Infosys and Wipro — entered the market.

We’ve got merch!

[[IMAGE:https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!MIZB!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8e3c5785-726a-4b65-9196-fc7c3fc026a2_2638x891.png]]

Pick up an Asterisk hat, tote bag, sweatshirt, or sticker pack in our online store and show off your good taste in writing and apparel. Featuring our new mascot, Ludwig, a rabbit-duck illusion popularized by Ludwig Wittgenstein in the 1950s, who reminds us that language derives its meaning from how it is used in practice.

For all of these players the beginnings were not particularly auspicious. Wipro had been founded as a cooking oil concern in the 1940s, and only pivoted to technology after its founder died and his young son was called back from a Stanford engineering degree. Infosys, for its part, waited a year to acquire its first telephone and three years to acquire its first computer; simply importing the minicomputer they eventually bought required fifty trips to Delhi.

It wasn’t long before all of these companies — TCS, HCL, CMC, Infosys, and Wipro — realized that the real money in information technology was not in hardware but in software. India had an abundance of excellent engineers, many of them graduates of the elite Indian Institutes of Technology system; and the wages they expected to earn were pitifully low compare to what American engineers might earn. And — a basic precondition for everything else — they spoke English. Why have your engineers build things and sell them, when you could just sell the engineering labor directly?

The problem, in the 1970s and ‘80s, was that this was simply difficult to do. All the way back in 1974 TCS had secured its first outsourced software contract, when a Detroit hospital had paid it to convert some accounting code from one dialect of COBOL to another. The task was simple enough. But TCS didn’t have any machines that could run the code, so its engineers developed the software on a secondhand Burroughs mainframe — acquired from the Life Insurance Corporation, whose communist unions had blocked its use for fear it would eliminate jobs — and wrote a filter to make ICL code run on Burroughs hardware. The finished code had to be physically shipped to the United States, since no data-communication links existed between the two countries.

TCS and the like still managed to secure outsourced engineering contracts; by 1987 Infosys was successful enough to have opened an office in Boston. But it was only around 1990 that the real money started rolling in.

There were two things that underwrote this great change of fortune. The first was physical infrastructure: undersea fiber-optic cables, laid in the early and middle years of the 1990s, made it much cheaper and much faster to transmit data between the various places of the world, and allowed for high-speed connections between India and the West. And the second was policy. In 1991, India faced a severe economic crisis, the culmination of a structural balance-of-payments deficit; at the peak of the emergency the Indian government was forced to airlift gold to London to secure emergency loans.

The ultimate response to the crisis, undertaken under the aegis of the reformist finance minister Manmohan Singh under the prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao, was to dismantle the “Licence Raj” that had defined the Indian state for decades. The onerous regulatory regime into which the Indian IT industry was born was dismantled; foreign investment was liberalized; and the Indian economy was, more or less, opened to the world. It was this combination of technological connectivity with economic liberalization, however limited, that underwrote everything that followed.

By the late 1990s the Indian IT sector had truly begun to shine. The catalyst was Y2K. Much of the world’s software had been written in the 1960s and ‘70s, most of it in the programming language COBOL, which stored years as two digits (such that “1968” was “68” and so on) in order to save on expensive memory. But this meant that when 1999 rolled into 2000, there was a risk that computers might interpret the year (“00”) not as 2000 but as 1900. Fixing this required the painstaking rewriting of millions of lines of COBOL: a grueling and labor-intensive endeavor, made more difficult by the fact that COBOL had been in decline among American developers for years.

But COBOL was still strong among Indian programmers, who had spent years dealing with clients like the Detroit hospital. And so in the late 1990s Indian programming talent enjoyed a sudden explosion of demand. By this point newer players, like Tech Mahindra and Cognizant, had joined the game; it was a gold rush for the writing and rewriting of dusty enterprise codebases. TCS alone remediated roughly 700 million lines of code. In 1999, Infosys became the first Indian company to be listed on the NASDAQ. India’s total software exports surged from $1 billion in 1997 to $6.2 billion by 2001.

It did not take too long for the humble startups of the 1970s and ‘80s to become economic giants. The 2000s and 2010s were a fantastic time for Indian IT and BPO: Broadband connectivity continued to improve; Indian IT firms were newly credible to Western purchasers thanks to the Y2K experience; and Western companies, under pressure to save money after the dot-com bust in the early 2000s and then again after the financial crisis of the late 2000s, found that offshoring work to India was an easy way to cut expenses. TCS crossed $1 billion in annual revenue in 2003, the first Indian IT company to do so; by 2012 it had surpassed $10 billion. Since its listing in 2004, TCS compounded revenue at roughly 15 percent a year. Infosys grew at a similar clip, reaching about $6 billion by fiscal year 2011.

And it was not only Indian IT firms that grew. Western companies increasingly set up their own captive operations in India — what are now called Global Capability Centers. India today hosts somewhere between 1,700 and 2,000 of these centers, the offshore arms of companies like JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Google, and Microsoft, employing roughly 1.9 million people.

And soon the same model was replicated for customer service and back-office work: It turned out there were countless simple functions that American and European businesses were eager to have done abroad for less money. In 1997, a General Electric executive named Pramod Bhasin opened GE Capital International Services in the city of Gurgaon, with 20 employees processing GE’s car loans; within four years the unit had expanded to 12,000 employees. In 2005 GECIS became an independent company and changed its name to Genpact; today it employs about 145,000 people.

And on top of this massive outsourcing boom, a small crop of massive companies emerged. By 2021, TCS, which in the early 2000s had absorbed CMC and consolidated its place as the dominant player in Indian IT, was valued at more than $200 billion; Infosys was valued at $100 billion; HCL and Cognizant at $50 billion; Wipro at $30 billion; and Tech Mahindra north of $20 billion. The IT companies were among the most valuable companies in India. Collectively, these six companies employed millions of people, with millions more employed at smaller players, or directly by Western firms.

In absolute terms, of course, the IT sector’s few million employees were a drop in the bucket: India has more than 250 million people working in agriculture alone, with hundreds of millions more employed in low-end informal services that have nothing to do wiht software. But the IT sector proved to be an invaluable anchor for the rest of the Indian economy. An IT worker paid $23,000 a year might have been ludicrously cheap by American standards; but he still earned several times India’s per capita GDP. His consumption — the cooks and maids he hired, the flights he bought, the money he infused into his town or his ancestral village — proved to be massively helpful for Indian growth in the 2000s and 2010s.

And indeed the Western stereotype of IT jobs as demeaning sweatshop labor was wrong. IT jobs were in extraordinarily high demand, and so the labor market for IT workers was extremely tight: In the fourth quarter of 2022 attrition at Infosys hit 27.7 percent, simply because employees had so many options that they could cycle between firms for 30 or 40 percent salary jumps. And an entire social infrastructure emerged around the dream of the Indian IT job. In the matrimonial pages of The Hindu, one of India’s most popular newspapers, the most desired type of job was “software engineer.”

The absolute peak of the IT model came in 2022. The pandemic and the resulting glut of digital spending had been a massive boon for TCS, Infosys, and their ilk; and accordingly they hired at a pace never seen before. TCS alone added nearly 100,000 employees in a single year; Infosys hired 85,000 graduates. The going was good.

The dimming of the IT dream

On November 30, 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT, a new chat interface for its GPT series of AI models. GitHub Copilot, which used a modified version of GPT-3, had become generally available the previous June. Initially, the capabilities of these tools were limited: The models would make simple mistakes of logic, or forget what it was doing, or confabulate something. But over time it became clear to everyone that the models would be very good at a wide range of economically valuable tasks. The work in which the Indian IT firms had specialized — routine code generation, application maintenance, and testing — could be done at an extremely low marginal cost, far below what even Infosys or Cognizant could offer.

The doubts arrived almost immediately. In February 2023 — less than three months after ChatGPT’s release — J. P. Morgan published a note warning that generative AI would be a “deflation driver” for legacy IT services, and that consulting firms like Accenture and Deloitte would gain market share over Infosys and Wipro. India’s own 2024 Economic Survey, presented to Parliament by the Finance Ministry, cautioned that AI “casts a huge pall of uncertainty as to its impact on workers across all skill levels,” and warned that employment in the BPO sector was “estimated to decline considerably in the next ten years.” By early 2026, the mood had turned to something closer to panic. At the India AI Impact Summit in New Delhi in February, the venture capitalist Vinod Khosla declared that IT services and BPO would “almost completely disappear within five years.” Less than two weeks later, the New York Times ran a long piece suggesting that AI is “starting to shrink.”

Investors’ expectations about the future prospects of the Indian IT industry have certainly soured: TCS, Cognizant, and Infosys have each shed about 30 percent of their market capitalization over the course of 2026. And — like many American tech companies — the Indian IT giants have started to shed workers. In July 2025, TCS announced the largest layoff in the history of Indian IT, releasing 12,000 employees in a single exercise. In 2024, headcount at Infosys fell for the first time in 22 years, and graduate hiring fell from 85,000 in 2022 to 12,000 in 2024. Wipro cut 25,000 jobs over two years; Cognizant announced “Project Leap,” a restructuring expected to cut about 15,000 jobs.

And this has been a disaster for the graduates on whom the IT firms have so long depended. IIT Delhi, the flagship university of the IIT system, saw its placement rate fall to 61 percent in 2025; across all 23 IIT campuses, roughly 8,000 students went unplaced, more than double the figure from two years earlier.

But there’s little sign, at least for the moment, that Indian IT companies are actually losing revenue because of AI. Revenue growth has slowed — from double digits a few years ago to low single digits in nominal terms — and overall headcount has been roughly flat. But there’s no sign of a collapse just yet. Margins at each of the major IT players have expanded over the last few years: In 2025, Infosys posted an operating margin of 21.1 percent, its best in three years. And, much like American tech companies, they are rebranding themselves as “AI-native”: TCS reported that it is already earning $2.3 billion in cash it labeled as “AI revenue.” A lot of this new AI business is concrete enough: A typical engagement might involve a Fortune 1000 company asking Infosys or TCS to build a retrieval-augmented generation tool on its internal data, or to integrate large language models into its existing enterprise workflows. The IT firms, in other words, are not being replaced by AI; they are being hired to implement it.

So the Indian IT firms are refashioning themselves to be somewhat more like American tech companies: lighter on labor and heavier on profit. And indeed they’re quite well-positioned to accomplish this pivot. India’s IT majors enjoy longstanding relationships with countless legacy enterprises; they’ve managed to gradually upskill themselves, moving from low-end programming gruntwork to higher-value work spanning cloud migration, cybersecurity, data analytics, and enterprise consulting; and in many cases they have more visibility into the work they do than any of their clients. In the future, if AI obviates the need for human programmers, Indian programmers will be as irrelevant as American ones; but in the immediate term, Infosys and the like are well-geared to expand their margins. Mohit Joshi, the CEO of Tech Mahindra, has described it as a shift from a “pyramid” to a “bulging middle”: fewer juniors at the base, more senior generalists working alongside AI tools, and a much smaller overall workforce generating more revenue per head. Revenue per employee at TCS rose to nearly $50,000 in fiscal year 2025; at Infosys, $60,000; at HCLTech, over $61,000.

So — at least for now — the Indian IT industry’s business is not collapsing; only its labor model is breaking. HCL’s CEO, C. Vijayakumar, suggested in February 2025 that “the time is out for that model”: The company would seek to “generate twice the revenue with half the workforce.” The decoupling of revenue and employee count “will happen and in the next few years, it will be much more pronounced.”

But this might not be the case in a few years.

If there’s any single type of company threatened by the prospect of powerful AI with superhuman coding abilities, it’s the companies selling cheap software labor. It’s for this reason that the huge semiconductor rally of the last year has been accompanied by a slump in the valuations of the Indian outsourcing firms: TCS, for example, is down more than 30 percent. It’s not that the IT giants are shriveling right now; but public markets seem to believe that the net present value of their cash flows are a good deal lower than they were a few months ago.

What if that comes to pass? What would that mean for the Indian IT dream?

The grim scenario is not hard to sketch. As AI models improve, the revenue that Indian IT firms earn from Western clients gradually declines: The work that once required fifty engineers now requires perhaps 10. (And even that is being generous.) So India sees its service exports, built up over decades of IT sector expansion, stagnate and eventually decline. At the same time, Indian firms themselves become consumers of AI: Through the medium of tokens they effectively import the outputs of American-owned models and American-owned compute. So India’s exports fall and its imports rise.

And perhaps this balance-of-payments erosion is mirrored by a weakening economic situation at home. The high-earning workers of the IT sector now sustain an enormous downstream economy of domestic consumption; as the ranks of the IT sector thin one could see the contraction ripple outwards into the rest of India’s economy, touching the many service workers whose livelihoods depend on their consumption.

For the tens of millions of Indians for whom IT was the pathway to a better life, and for the Indian economy more broadly, the question is a simple and disturbing one: What then?
